instruction: What major processes are included in the RAM model for ring current-atmosphere interactions?
output: Ring current-atmosphere interactions model (RAM) [Jordanova et al., 1994, 2006; 2012] • Solves bounce-averaged Boltzmann equation for distribution functions of ions and electrons • Includes all major loss processes • Convection and corotation E field • Flexible B field options

instruction: What are the improvements made in the SCB solution according to Engel et al. (2019)?
output: Recent Improvements [Engel et al., 2019] • SCB grid decoupled from RAM grid • Improved convergence of SCB solution, especially during very active periods • Adaptive SCB coupling frequency • Improved numerics throughout

instruction: How does the RAM model address ionospheric potential and conductance changes?
output: Self-consistent Electric Field [Yu et al., 2017] • RAM provides FAC and precipitation • Precipitation drives conductance changes, solve for ionospheric potential • SCE shown to capture occurrence of SAPS

instruction: What boundary conditions are required for RAM-SCB in the SWMF model according to Welling et al. (2018)?
output: Coupling with SHIELDS/SWMF RAM-SCBE as a drop-in IM component in SWMF • Coupled physics models − Global MHD: BATSRUS − Ionospheric electrodynamics: RIM − Inner magnetosphere: RAM-SCB • Driven by solar wind state at upstream boundary − Geospace model boundary at 32R E upstream − Provides required boundary conditions for RAM-SCB

instruction: What license is RAM-SCB-E published under and where can it be accessed?
output: RAM-SCB-E is provided as open-source software − Repository at https://github.com/lanl/RAM-SCB − 3-clause BSD license

instruction: What are the types of data that improve nowcasts and hindcasts in RAM?
output: Data Assimilation Using data to improve nowcast/hindcast states • Ensemble Kalman Filter − EnKF is computationally cheaper than some other DA schemes − Orthonormal projection used to capture dominant correlations in ring current − Data assimilation is performed in orthonormal subspace and then transformed back into RAM frame − Uses covariance inflation to avoid ensemble collapse and localization to reduce spurious long range correlation

instruction: How does SHIELDS-RC utilize statistical models for real-time forecasting?
output: Real Time Prediction and Forecasting SHIELDS-RC provides nowcasts and short-range forecasts • Simplified configuration − All boundary conditions must be specified into the future to enable prediction Generally this means models parameterized by geomagnetic indices − Can use dipole field or Kp-parameterized T89

instruction: What are the visualization and analysis capabilities provided by SpacePy for the RAM-SCB model?
output: Visualization and Analysis Post-processing to VTK format • Visualization and Analysis tools for most products provided in SpacePy − See spacepy.pybats.ram • Postprocessing tools generate VTK products from RAM-SCB restart files − VTK is open-source and compatible with tools such as ParaView, VisIt, PyVista, MayaVi, and more...

instruction: What were the absolute calibration accuracies achieved in the FT-IR spectroscopy measurements of 17O-enriched CO2 in the m3 region?
output: We report new Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy measurements of the 17O-enriched isotopologues of CO2 in the m3 region (2200-2450 cm-1, 65-75 THz) with absolute calibration accuracies better than 3 × 10-6 cm-1 (~100 kHz) for strong, isolated transitions.

instruction: What spectroscopic constants were reported for the isotopologues 16O12C17O, 17O12C17O, and 17O12C18O?

instruction: Which instrument was used for the FT-IR spectroscopy measurements reported in this study?

instruction: What is the significance of the transition frequencies obtained for the study of planetary atmospheres?

instruction: What measures were taken to achieve high performance in the JPL-FTS during the spectroscopy measurements?

instruction: What zones have astronomers marked around super hot stars that affect cooler stars' planet formation?
output: Astronomers have laid down the cosmic equivalent of yellow 'caution' tape around super hot stars, marking the zones where cooler stars are in danger of having their developing planets blasted away.

instruction: What distance from hot stars ensures cooler stars can safely form planets?
output: The results show that cooler stars are safe as long as they lie beyond about 1.6 light-years, or nearly 10 trillion miles, of any hot stars.

instruction: What does the research reveal about the fate of protoplanetary disks in the danger zone of an O-star?
output: In addition, the new study indicates that a protoplanetary disk will boil off faster in the zone's perilous core.

instruction: What effect does an O-star have on protoplanetary disks over time?
output: Previous studies revealed that these protoplanetary disks can be destroyed by the most massive, hottest type of star in the universe, called an O-star, over a period of about a million years.

instruction: What is the primary finding of the Spitzer Space Telescope regarding the Rosette Nebula?

instruction: How many stars in the Rosette Nebula have protoplanetary disks within the danger zone of an O-star?
output: Within this distance, only 27 percent of the stars had disks, with fewer and fewer disks spotted around stars closest to the O-star.

instruction: What happens to protoplanetary disks that enter the danger zone of an O-star?
output: For example, a disk two times closer to an O-star than another disk will evaporate twice as fast.

instruction: What is the significance of the distance 10 trillion miles from an O-star?
output: The observations revealed that, beyond 10 trillion miles of an O-star, about 45 percent of the stars had disks -- about the same amount as there were in safer neighborhoods free of O-stars.

instruction: What do astronomers believe may have happened to our sun in relation to O-stars?
output: Some astronomers think our sun was born in a similarly violent neighborhood studded with O-stars before migrating to its present, more spacious home.

instruction: Who led the study on planetary danger zones and which journal did it appear in?
output: 'Stars move around all the time, so if one wanders into the danger zone and stays for too long, it will probably never be able to form planets,' said Zoltan Balog of the University of Arizona, Tucson, lead author of the new report, appearing May 20 in the Astrophysical Journal.

instruction: What are protoplanetary disks and how do they form?

instruction: What role does ultraviolet radiation from an O-star play in protoplanetary disk dynamics?
output: Ultraviolet radiation from an O-star heats and evaporates the dust and gas in the disk, then winds from the star blow the material away.

instruction: How do cooler stars decay over time in relation to their proximity to hot stars?

instruction: What imaging technique did NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter use to create a 3-D reconstruction of ancient water channels on Mars?
output: NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has provided images allowing scientists for the first time to create a 3-D reconstruction of ancient water channels below the martian surface.

instruction: What is significant about the flooding channels attributed to catastrophic flooding on Mars in the last 500 million years?
output: The spacecraft took numerous images during the past few years that showed channels attributed to catastrophic flooding in the last 500 million years. During this period, Mars had been otherwise considered cold and dry. These channels are essential to understanding the extent to which recent hydrologic activity prevailed during such arid conditions.

instruction: What role did the Shallow Radar (SHARAD) play in the research of the Marte Vallis channel system?
output: To probe the length, width, and depth of these underground channels, the researchers used the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's Shallow Radar (SHARAD).

instruction: How do the findings related to Marte Vallis compare to the Chryse basin channels regarding their formation?
output: Marte Vallis' morphology is similar to more ancient channel systems on Mars, especially those of the Chryse basin. Many scientists think the Chryse channels likely were formed by the catastrophic release of groundwater, although others suggest lava can produce many of the same features. In comparison, little is known about Marte Vallis.

instruction: What evidence did the SHARAD radar provide about the phases of channel formation in Elysium Planitia?
output: With the SHARAD radar, the team was able to map the buried channels in three dimensions with enough detail to see evidence suggesting two different phases of channel formation.

instruction: What did Gareth Morgan state about the scale of erosion that created the channels?
output: Our findings show the scale of erosion that created the channels previously was underestimated and the channel depth was at least twice that of previous approximations.

instruction: What geological feature is linked to the origins of the floods that created the channels?
output: The mapping also provided sufficient information to establish the floods that carved the channels originated from a now-buried portion of the Cerberus Fossae fracture system.

instruction: What did Lynn Carter explain about the radar reflectors found in the data?
output: In this region, the radar picked up multiple ‘reflectors,' which are surfaces or boundaries that reflect radio waves, so it was possible to see multiple layers,.

instruction: What unique information did the radar provide regarding the history of water on Mars?
output: While the radar was probing thick layers of dry, solid rock, it provided us with unique information about the recent history of water in a key region of Mars.

instruction: Who were the key contributors to the findings reported in the March 7 issue of Science Express?

instruction: What are the characteristics of Comet 73P/Schwassman-Wachmann 3 as observed by the Spitzer Space Telescope?
output: This infrared image from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope shows the broken Comet 73P/Schwassman-Wachmann 3 skimming along a trail of debris left during its multiple trips around the sun. The flame-like objects are the comet's fragments and their tails, while the dusty comet trail is the line bridging the fragments.

instruction: What caused Comet 73P/Schwassman-Wachmann 3 to break apart?
output: Comet 73P /Schwassman-Wachmann 3 began to splinter apart in 1995 during one of its voyages around the sweltering sun. Since then, the comet has continued to disintegrate into dozens of fragments, at least 36 of which can be seen here. Astronomers believe the icy comet cracked due the thermal stress from the sun.

instruction: What is the significance of the Spitzer Space Telescope's image of Comet 73P/Schwassman-Wachmann 3?
output: The Spitzer image provides the best look yet at the trail of debris left in the comet's wake after its 1995 breakup. The observatory's infrared eyes were able to see the dusty comet bits and pieces, which are warmed by sunlight and glow at infrared wavelengths. This comet debris ranges in size from pebbles to large boulders.

instruction: How does the debris from Comet 73P/Schwassman-Wachmann 3 contribute to meteor showers on Earth?
output: When Earth passes near this rocky trail every year, the comet rubble burns up in our atmosphere, lighting up the sky in meteor showers. In 2022, Earth is expected to cross close to the comet's trail, producing a noticeable meteor shower.

instruction: What happens to sun-like stars when they die according to the Spitzer observations?

instruction: How does the Large Magellanic Cloud contribute to our understanding of star formation?

instruction: What elements are considered 'heavy metals' in the context of the Large Magellanic Cloud?

instruction: How is star birth related to the death of massive stars in Henize 206?

instruction: What phenomenon associated with the cluster Abell 383 allows for the observation of distant galaxies?
output: The giant cluster of elliptical galaxies in the center of this image contains so much dark matter mass that its gravity bends light. This means that for very distant galaxies in the background, the clusters gravitational field acts as a sort of magnifying glass, bending and concentrating the distant objects light towards Hubble. These gravitational lenses are one tool astronomers can use to extend Hubbles vision beyond what it would normally be capable of observing.

instruction: What specific galaxy has been identified by astronomers using Abell 383 as a gravitational lens?
output: Using Abell 383, a team of astronomers have identified and studied a galaxy so far away we see it as it was less than a billion years after the Big Bang. It is visible as two tiny dots (labelled) on either side of the bright cluster galaxy in the centre. Distant objects seen through gravitational lenses are typically multiply imaged and heavily distorted.

instruction: What significant characteristics were discovered about the distant galaxy observed through Abell 383?
output: Viewing this galaxy through the gravitational lens meant that the scientists were able to discern many intriguing features that would otherwise have remained hidden, including that its stars were unexpectedly old for a galaxy this close in time to the beginning of the Universe. This has profound implications for our understanding of how and when the first galaxies formed, and how the diffuse fog of neutral hydrogen that filled the early Universe was cleared.

instruction: What is the actual shape of raindrops as explained in the GPM video?
output: Raindrops are actually shaped like the top of a hamburger bun, round on the top and flat on the bottom. This new video from the Global Precipitation Measurement mission explains why.

instruction: How do dust and smoke particles in clouds contribute to raindrop formation?
output: Way up high in the atmosphere, dust and smoke particles suspended in clouds create places where moisture can settle and form into drops. The drops sitting up here are like little globes of water, nearly round and spherical.

instruction: What affects the shape of raindrops as they fall according to size?
output: Small raindrops, less than 1 millimeter in size (less than one-sixteenth of an inch), retain a roughly rounded shape because of surface tension, but drops can collide into each other as they are falling and form bigger raindrops.

instruction: What happens to drops larger than 4.5 millimeters during their fall?
output: Drops that grow larger than 4.5 millimeters (about three-sixteenths of an inch) become distorted into a parachute-shape as they fall, and then eventually they break up into smaller drops.

instruction: What instruments are used by the GPM Core Observatory to measure precipitation?
output: The Core Observatory will has two precipitation-measuring instruments, the multi-channel GPM Microwave Imager and the Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar, designed and built by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA, and Japan's National Institute of Information and Communications Technology.

instruction: How often is rainfall and snowfall data returned by the GPM mission?
output: GPM is an international satellite mission led by NASA and JAXA. It will return data on rainfall and snowfall, which will be used for weather forecasts and climate studies, as well as other applications, everywhere around the world every three hours.

instruction: What role does surface tension play in the shape of raindrops?
output: Raindrops form into this shape because of the surface tension of water, which is sometimes described as a 'skin' that makes the water molecules stick together.

instruction: How does airflow affect the shape of falling raindrops based on their size?
output: Drops that are 2 to 3 millimeters (just under one-eighth of an inch) in size are big enough to be affected by air pushing against them as they fall.

instruction: What is the primary focus of the Global Precipitation Measurement mission?
output: The upcoming Global Precipitation Measurement mission will study the sizes of raindrops layer by layer within clouds with a new advanced radar aboard the GPM Core Observatory, scheduled to launch from Japan in early 2014.

instruction: What misconception about raindrop shape does the GPM video address?
output: When asked to picture the shape of raindrops, many of us will imagine water looking like tears that fall from our eyes, or the stretched out drip from a leaky faucet. This popular misconception is often reinforced in weather imagery associated with predictions and forecasts.

instruction: What is the age of the young stars in the star cluster NGC 1333?
output: NGC 1333 is a star cluster populated with many young stars that are less than 2 million years old -- a blink of an eye in astronomical terms for stars like these expected to burn for billions of years.

instruction: Which observatories contributed data to the composite image of NGC 1333?

instruction: How many young stars were detected by Chandra in the NGC 1333 star cluster?
output: The Chandra data reveal 95 young stars glowing in X-ray light, 41 of which had not been seen previously using Spitzer because they lacked infrared emission from a surrounding disk.

instruction: What was the primary focus of the study conducted by Elaine Winston and her team?
output: To make a detailed study of the X-ray properties of young stars, a team of astronomers, led by Elaine Winston from the University of Exeter, United Kingdom, analyzed the Chandra X-ray data of both NGC 1333, located about 780 light-years from Earth, and the Serpens cloud, a similar cluster of young stars about 1,100 light-years away.

instruction: How does the X-ray brightness of stars in NGC 1333 depend on their physical characteristics?
output: The researchers found that the X-ray brightness of the stars in NGC 1333 and the Serpens cloud depends on the total brightness of the stars across the electromagnetic spectrum, as found in previous studies of other clusters. They also found that the X-ray brightness mainly depends on the size of the star.

instruction: Who manages the Spitzer Space Telescope mission?

instruction: In what publication were the results of the study published?

instruction: What does the data from Chandra reveal about previously undetected young stars?
output: The Chandra data reveal 95 young stars glowing in X-ray light, 41 of which had not been seen previously using Spitzer because they lacked infrared emission from a surrounding disk.

instruction: What is the relationship between star size and X-ray brightness?
output: In other words, the bigger the stellar sparkler, the brighter it will glow in X-rays.

instruction: What institutions manage the Chandra X-ray Observatory and its operations?

instruction: What did NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope reveal about the state of the Cassiopeia A neutron star?
output: The surprising finding indicates Cassiopeia A, the remnant of a star that died in a supernova explosion 325 years ago, is not resting peacefully. Instead, this dead star likely shot out at least one burst of energy as recently as 50 years ago.

instruction: What is the significance of the light echo captured by Spitzer around Cassiopeia A?
output: The echo from Cassiopeia A is the first witnessed around a long-dead star and the largest ever seen. It was discovered by accident during a Spitzer instrument test.

instruction: How did astronomers interpret the unusual activity of the Cassiopeia A neutron star?
output: Typically, a star that has recently died will continue to act up. Consequently, astronomers were puzzled that the star responsible for Cassiopeia A appeared to be silent so soon after its death.

instruction: What type of astronomical object could the Cassiopeia A neutron star potentially be classified as?
output: The new infrared echo indicates the Cassiopeia A neutron star is active and may even be an exotic, spastic type of object called a magnetar.

instruction: What features did astronomers observe in the Spitzer images indicating the presence of light echoes?
output: Astronomers first saw hints of the infrared echo in strange, tangled dust features that showed up in the Spitzer test image.

instruction: What was indicated by the follow-up observations made by ground-based telescopes after the initial Spitzer findings?

instruction: What was revealed about the dust in Cassiopeia A during follow-up observations taken one year later?

instruction: Who were the lead authors of the study concerning the discovery of Cassiopeia A's light echo?

instruction: Which instrument of the Spitzer Space Telescope was responsible for making the new observations of Cassiopeia A?

instruction: What previous assumption about the Cassiopeia A neutron star was challenged by Spitzer's findings?
output: We had thought the stellar remains inside Cassiopeia A were just fading away.

instruction: How does the concept of a magnetar relate to the findings about Cassiopeia A?

instruction: What impact did the findings from the Spitzer observations have on understanding neutron stars like Cassiopeia A?

instruction: What does the observation of NGC 6240 reveal about galaxy mergers?
output: This image of a pair of colliding galaxies called NGC 6240 shows them in a rare, short-lived phase of their evolution just before they merge into a single, larger galaxy. The prolonged, violent collision has drastically altered the appearance of both galaxies and created huge amounts of heat -- turning NGC 6240 into an "infrared luminous" active galaxy.

instruction: What is significant about NGC 6240 in relation to active galaxies?
output: A rich variety of active galaxies, with different shapes, luminosities and radiation profiles exist. These galaxies may be related -- astronomers have suspected that they may represent an evolutionary sequence. By catching different galaxies in different stages of merging, a story emerges as one type of active galaxy changes into another. NGC 6240 provides an important "missing link" in this process.

instruction: What instruments were used to capture the image of NGC 6240?
output: This image was created from combined data from the infrared array camera of NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope at 3.6 and 8.0 microns (red) and visible light from NASA's Hubble Space Telescope (green and blue).

instruction: What is the primary mission objective of the Mars 2020 rover?
output: The Mars 2020 rover will investigate a region of Mars where the ancient environment may have been favorable for microbial life, probing the martian rocks for evidence of past life. Throughout its investigation, it will collect samples of soil and rock, and cache them on the surface for potential return to Earth by a future mission.

instruction: How will the Mars 2020 rover explore for signs of past life on Mars?
output: Two science instruments mounted on the rover's robotic arm will be used to search for signs of past life and determine where to collect samples by analyzing the chemical, mineral, physical, and organic characteristics of martian rocks.

instruction: What innovations are included in the landing system of the Mars 2020 rover compared to Curiosity?
output: The Mars 2020 rover will use the same sky crane landing system as Curiosity, but will have the ability to land in more challenging terrain with two enhancements, making more rugged sites eligible as safe landing candidates.

instruction: What will happen to the samples collected by the Mars 2020 rover?
output: About 30 of these sample tubes will be deposited at select locations for return on a potential future sample-retrieval mission. In laboratories on Earth, specimens from Mars could be analyzed for evidence of past life on Mars and possible health hazards for future human missions.

instruction: What is the significance of the range trigger in the Mars 2020 rover's landing system?
output: By adding what's known as range trigger, we can specify where we want the parachute to open, not just at what velocity we want it to open. That shrinks our landing area by nearly half.

instruction: What are the phases involved in the development of the Mars 2020 mission?
output: Once a mission receives preliminary approval, it must go through four rigorous technical and programmatic reviews — known as Key Decision Points (KDP) — to proceed through the phases of development prior to launch. Phase A involves concept and requirements definition, Phase B is preliminary design and technology development, Phase C is final design and fabrication, and Phase D is system assembly, testing, and launch.

instruction: What types of instruments will the Mars 2020 rover carry for analyzing Martian terrain?
output: On the rover's mast, two science instruments will provide high-resolution imaging and three types of spectroscopy for characterizing rocks and soil from a distance, also helping to determine which rock targets to explore up close.

instruction: What is the purpose of the microphones on the Mars 2020 rover?
output: Microphones have flown on previous missions to Mars, including NASA's Phoenix Mars Lander in 2008, but never have actually been used on the surface of the Red Planet. This will be a great opportunity for the public to hear the sounds of Mars for the first time, and it could also provide useful engineering information.

instruction: How does the Mars 2020 rover plan to assess subsurface geological structures?
output: A ground-penetrating radar will assess subsurface geologic structure.

instruction: What capability does the terrain-relative navigation provide for the Mars 2020 rover during its descent?
output: Terrain-relative navigation on the new rover will use onboard analysis of downward-looking images taken during descent, matching them to a map that indicates zones designated unsafe for landing. As it is descending, the spacecraft can tell whether it is headed for one of the unsafe zones and divert to safe ground nearby.

instruction: What geological feature on Mars is inferred to be formed by contemporary flowing water?
output: These dark, narrow, 100-meter-long (328-foot-long) streaks called recurring slope lineae flowing downhill on Mars are inferred to have been formed by contemporary flowing water.

instruction: What significant discovery about water on Mars was reported by NASA on September 29, 2015?
output: New findings from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) provide the strongest evidence yet that liquid water flows intermittently on present-day Mars.

instruction: Which instrument on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter was used to detect signatures of hydrated minerals?
output: Using an imaging spectrometer on MRO, researchers detected signatures of hydrated minerals on slopes where mysterious streaks are seen on the Red Planet.

instruction: What seasonal conditions are necessary for the dark streaks on Mars to appear?
output: They appear in several locations on Mars when temperatures are above -23°C (-10°F), and disappear at colder times.

instruction: What is the role of hydrated salts in the context of recurring slope lineae on Mars?
output: The hydrated salts would lower the freezing point of a liquid brine, just as salt on roads here on Earth causes ice and snow to melt more rapidly.

instruction: What is the interpretation of spectral signatures detected on Mars's dark streaks?
output: Ojha and his co-authors interpret the spectral signatures as caused by hydrated minerals called perchlorates.

instruction: Which mission first documented recurring slope lineae at multiple sites on Mars?
output: HiRISE observations now have documented RSL at dozens of sites on Mars.

instruction: Which specific hydrated minerals were identified in the study of RSL on Mars?
output: The hydrated salts most consistent with the chemical signatures are likely a mixture of magnesium perchlorate, magnesium chlorate, and sodium perchlorate.

instruction: How do perchlorates affect the freezing point of liquids on Mars?
output: Some perchlorates have been shown to keep liquids from freezing even when conditions are as cold as -70°C (-94°F).

instruction: What does John Grunsfeld say about the significance of the discoveries related to water on Mars?
output: Our quest on Mars has been to ‘follow the water,' in our search for life in the universe, and now we have convincing science that validates what we've long suspected.

instruction: Which scientific instruments have previously detected perchlorates on Mars?
output: NASA's Phoenix lander and Curiosity rover both found them in the planet's soil.

instruction: What advancement does Michael Meyer highlight regarding water on Mars?
output: It seems that the more we study Mars, the more we learn how life could be supported and where there are resources to support life in the future.

instruction: What evidence supports the liquid water-formation hypotheses for recurring slope lineae?
output: This is the first spectral detection that unambiguously supports our liquid water-formation hypotheses for RSL.

instruction: What was the primary source of the hydrated salts detected in the study?
output: We found the hydrated salts only when the seasonal features were widest, which suggests that either the dark streaks themselves or a process that forms them is the source of the hydration.

instruction: What is the significance of the Orion Nebula in star formation?
output: The Orion nebula, our closest massive star-making factory, is located 1,450 light-years from Earth. It contains about 1,000 young stars that illuminate a cold cloud of gas and dust, creating beautiful nebulosity.

instruction: What are the characteristics of the massive stars in the Orion Nebula?
output: In the center of the nebula are four monstrously massive stars, up to 100,000 times as luminous as our sun, called the Trapezium. Radiation and winds from these stars are blasting gas and dust away.

instruction: What does the infrared image from the Spitzer Space Telescope reveal about the Orion Nebula?
output: This infrared image from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope shows the Orion nebula, surrounded by a ring of dust, and reveals the presence of young stars and regions of star formation.

instruction: How many stars and stellar embryos did Spitzer find in the Orion cloud complex?
output: Within the Orion cloud complex, the Spitzer Space Telescope found 2,300 stars circled by disks of planet-forming dust and 200 stellar embryos too young to have developed disks.

instruction: What is observed in different wavelength bands of the infrared light from the Orion Nebula?
output: Light with wavelengths of 8 and 5.8 microns comes mainly from dust heated by starlight, 4.5 microns shows hot gas and dust, and 3.6 microns is from starlight.

instruction: What role does the Spitzer Space Telescope play in studying the Orion Nebula?
output: Spitzer surveyed a significant swath of the Orion constellation, providing insights about star formation and capturing infrared light that reveals detailed structures.

instruction: What types of material are found in the Orion Nebula according to the Spitzer observations?
output: Dark veins that contain embryonic stars appear against the pinkish nebulosity, while jets of gas from the stars create green horseshoe-shaped globs in the cloud.

instruction: What was the date of the observation of the Orion Nebula by Spitzer?
output: The observation of the Orion Nebula took place on August 14th, 2006.

instruction: What is the distance of the Orion Nebula from Earth?
output: The Orion Nebula is located 1,450 light-years from Earth.

instruction: What instruments did the Spitzer Space Telescope use to capture the image of the Orion Nebula?
output: This image shows infrared light captured by Spitzer's infrared array camera.

instruction: What instruments and sensors are used by Robbie Hood during hurricane flights?
output: Hood, an atmospheric scientist at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, has flown several times into the fury of the whirling storms. She claims it's actually not as scary as it sounds. There is plenty to look at on her laptop, however, which displays a continuous stream of real-time atmospheric data being collected by an array of instruments and sensors outside the aircraft. The goal is to use the data to improve understanding and prediction of hurricanes.

instruction: How does rainfall intensity affect hurricane strength according to Robbie Hood's research?
output: Specifically, Hood is interested in how rainfall intensity affects overall storm strength. (When water vapor condenses into rain, energy is released to the surrounding air.) The research conducted by Hood and her colleagues helps models more accurately predict a hurricane's track, strength at landfall and potential for inland flooding.

instruction: What advantages does aircraft data provide over satellite observations in hurricane research?
output: But why send an airplane into the middle of a hurricane when there are satellites that can make observations from space? Hood says that the aircraft data, when combined with satellite information, gives scientists a more detailed, three-dimensional view of how hurricanes work. Measurements taken from inside the storm are also used to verify the accuracy of the satellite data.

instruction: What personal background inspires Robbie Hood's interest in studying hurricanes?
output: Hood's fascination with weather and hurricanes goes back to her days growing up in the South. Raised on a cattle farm in Missouri, she became very familiar with the economic impact weather can have on agriculture.

instruction: What experiences influenced Robbie Hood’s perception of hurricane damage?
output: Hood's family also happened to be in Mississippi when, in 1969, Hurricane Camille slammed into the Gulf Coast. "To see the kind of damage that it could do made a big impression on me," said Hood, who remembers the storm knocking out power, downing trees, and blowing the roofs off of houses.

instruction: In what way does Robbie Hood compare hurricanes to people?
output: In fact, Hood has always been a bit of a people person. "I credit my Native American heritage with my intense interest and appreciation of people," said Hood, who is a member of the western tribe of the Cherokee nation. "I think I like studying hurricanes because they act so much like people. Hurricanes have names and personalities and don't behave like we expect them to sometimes."

instruction: What is the primary goal of the Convection and Moisture Experiment missions led by Robbie Hood?
output: Hood served as lead scientist on two of NASA's hurricane-probing CAMEX (Convection And Moisture Experiment) missions. The goal is to use the data to improve understanding and prediction of hurricanes.

instruction: What is Robbie Hood's profession and her involvement in hurricane research?
output: Robbie Hood, an atmospheric scientist at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, has flown several times into the fury of the whirling storms.

instruction: How does Robbie Hood describe the view from the aircraft when flying through hurricanes?
output: Hood, who served as lead scientist on two of NASA's hurricane-probing CAMEX (Convection And Moisture Experiment) missions, said, "The view out of the aircraft windows can be somewhat boring,". The aircraft is often flying through clouds so there is not much to see.

output: The goal is to use the data to improve understanding and prediction of hurricanes.

instruction: What significant step toward deep space exploration did China achieve on December 2, 2013 with the launch of the Chang'e-3 lunar probe?
output: China launched the Chang'e-3 lunar probe with the country's first Moon rover onboard early on December 2, marking a significant step toward deep space exploration.

instruction: What was the primary purpose of the Chang'e-3 mission according to Wu Weiren, the lunar program's chief designer?
output: The probe's soft-landing is the most difficult task during the mission, said Wu Weiren, the lunar program's chief designer. "This will be a breakthrough for China to realize zero-distance observation and survey on the Moon."

instruction: What will the Chang'e-3 Moon rover named Yutu be tasked with during its mission?
output: Scheduled tasks for the Moon rover include surveying the Moon's geological structure and surface substances, while looking for natural resources.

instruction: How did the Chang'e-3 mission contribute to China's lunar program?
output: Chang'e-3 is part of the second phase of China's lunar program, which includes orbiting, landing, and returning to Earth. It follows the success of the Chang'e-1 and Chang'e-2 missions in 2007 and 2010.

instruction: What technologies were highlighted as newly developed for the Chang'e-3 mission?
output: Weiren added that more than 80% of the technologies and products used by the mission are newly developed.

instruction: What is the expected timeline for the third step of China's lunar program?
output: China is likely to realize the third step of its lunar program in 2017, which is to land a lunar probe on the Moon, release a Moon rover, and return the probe to Earth.

instruction: What was the significance of Chang'e-2 in relation to the Chang'e-3 mission?
output: Launched on October 1, 2010, Chang'e-2 verified some crucial technologies for Chang'e-3 and reconnoitered the landing area.

instruction: What major tasks did the Chang'e-1 mission achieve before crashing onto the lunar surface?
output: After orbiting for 494 days and intentionally crashing onto the lunar surface, Chang'e-1 sent back 1.37 terabytes of data, producing China's first complete Moon picture.

instruction: What does Sun Huixian, deputy engineer-in-chief, say about the future of China's space exploration?

instruction: What cooperative stance did Li Benzheng mention regarding China's lunar program in relation to India's space efforts?

instruction: What is the significance of the discovery of Sedna in relation to the Oort cloud?
output: This is likely the first detection of the long-hypothesized "Oort cloud," a faraway repository of small icy bodies that supplies the comets that streak by Earth.

instruction: What are the size and distance characteristics of Sedna compared to Pluto?
output: After Mars, it is the second reddest object in the solar system. It is estimated Sedna is approximately three-fourths the size of Pluto. Sedna is likely the largest object found in the solar system since Pluto was discovered in 1930.

instruction: How was Sedna discovered and what instruments were used?
output: Brown, along with Drs. Chad Trujillo of the Gemini Observatory, Hawaii, and David Rabinowitz of Yale University, New Haven, Conn., found the planet-like object, or planetoid, on Nov. 14, 2003. The researchers used the 48-inch Samuel Oschin Telescope at Caltech's Palomar Observatory near San Diego.

instruction: What temperature conditions exist in the region where Sedna is located?
output: Sedna is extremely far from the Sun, in the coldest known region of our solar system, where temperatures never rise above minus 240 degrees Celsius (minus 400 degrees Fahrenheit).

instruction: What are the implications of Sedna's orbit for understanding the early solar system?
output: The elliptical orbit of Sedna is unlike anything previously seen by astronomers. However, it resembles that of objects predicted to lie in the hypothetical Oort cloud. Brown said this "inner Oort cloud" may have been formed by gravity from a rogue star near the Sun in the solar system's early days.

instruction: What evidence exists regarding the potential for Sedna having a moon?
output: Rabinowitz said there is indirect evidence that Sedna may have a moon. The researchers hope to check this possibility with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope.

instruction: What are scientists currently investigating about the surface composition of Sedna?
output: Trujillo has begun to examine the object's surface with one of the world's largest optical/infrared telescopes, the 8-meter (26-foot) Frederick C. Gillett Gemini Telescope on Mauna Kea, Hawaii. "We still don't understand what is on the surface of this body. It is nothing like what we would have predicted or what we can explain," he said.

instruction: What predictions are made about Sedna's visibility in the future?
output: Sedna will become closer and brighter over the next 72 years, before it begins its 10,500-year trip to the far reaches of the solar system.

instruction: How do astronomers measure the distance from a star to the inner edge of its protoplanetary disk?
output: Researchers are interested in calculating how far young stars are from the inner edge of their surrounding protoplanetary disks. These disks of gas and dust are sites where planets form over the course of millions of years.

instruction: What is the significance of the study published in the Astrophysical Journal regarding YLW 16B?
output: Meng is the first author on a new study published in the Astrophysical Journal using data from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope and four ground-based telescopes to determine the distance from a star to the inner rim of its surrounding protoplanetary disk.

instruction: What method do researchers use to measure light echoes from protoplanetary disks?
output: Researchers used a method called 'photo-reverberation,' also known as 'light echoes.' When the central star brightens, some of the light hits the surrounding disk, causing a delayed 'echo.'

instruction: What does the light echo measurement reveal about the protoplanetary disk studied?
output: Researchers were able to determine that the inner edge is relatively thick.

instruction: What star was observed in this study to measure protoplanetary disk distances?
output: The star used in this study is called YLW 16B and lies about 400 light-years from Earth.

instruction: What previous techniques had astronomers used to measure the size of accretion disks around supermassive black holes?
output: Previously, astronomers had used the light echo technique to measure the size of accretion disks of material around supermassive black holes.

instruction: What is the purpose of studying protoplanetary disks in relation to exoplanets?
output: 'Understanding protoplanetary disks can help us understand some of the mysteries about exoplanets, the planets in solar systems outside our own,' said Huan Meng.

instruction: How does the new light echo method differ when applied to protoplanetary disks versus accretion disks?
output: While light echoes from supermassive black holes represent delays of days to weeks, scientists measured the light echo from the protoplanetary disk in this study to be a mere 74 seconds.

instruction: What telescopes contributed to the data collected in the study of YLW 16B?
output: Astronomers combined Spitzer data with observations from ground-based telescopes: the Mayall telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona; the SOAR and SMARTS telescopes in Chile; and the Harold L. Johnson telescope in Mexico.

instruction: What are the challenges faced by astronomers when monitoring YLW 16B?
output: Because of thick interstellar clouds that block the view from Earth, astronomers could not use visible light to monitor the star.

instruction: What observations did the Spitzer Space Telescope make of the Helix Nebula?

instruction: What is the distance of the Helix Nebula from Earth?

instruction: How are planetary nebulae formed?
output: Planetary nebulae are actually the remains of stars that once looked a lot like our sun. When sun-like stars die, they puff out their outer gaseous layers.

instruction: What role do comets play in the formation of dust in the Helix Nebula?

instruction: What significant discovery was made using the Spitzer Space Telescope regarding newborn stars?
output: Astronomers have at last uncovered newborn stars at the frenzied center of our Milky Way galaxy. The discovery was made using the infrared vision of NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope.

instruction: What makes the center of the Milky Way galaxy difficult for star formation?
output: The heart of our spiral galaxy is cluttered with stars, dust and gas, and at its very center, a supermassive black hole. Conditions there are harsh, with fierce stellar winds, powerful shock waves and other factors that make it difficult for stars to form.

instruction: How did astronomers identify young stellar objects in the galactic center?
output: Ramirez and colleagues began their search by scanning large Spitzer mosaics of our galactic center. They narrowed in on more than 100 candidates, but needed more detailed data to confirm the stars' identities.

instruction: What characteristics did scientists look for in the light of candidate stars to distinguish young stars from older ones?
output: To sort through the confusion, the astronomers looked at their candidate stars with Spitzer's spectrograph - an instrument that breaks light apart to reveal its rainbow-like array of infrared colors. Molecules around stars leave imprints in their light, which the spectrograph can detect.

instruction: What did the spectral analysis reveal about the three stars identified in the study?
output: The results revealed three stars with clear signs of youth, for example, certain warm, dense gases. These youthful features are found in other places in the galaxy where stars are being formed.

instruction: What is significant about the age and environment of the young stellar objects found by astronomers?
output: The young stellar objects are all less than about 1 million years old. They are embedded in cocoons of gas and dust, which will eventually flatten to disks that, according to theory, later lump together to form planets.

instruction: Who was the principal investigator of the research program related to the discovery of newborn stars?
output: 'These stars are like needles in a haystack,' said Solange Ramirez, the principal investigator of the research program at NASA's Exoplanet Science Institute at the California Institute of Technology, Pasadena.

instruction: What challenges did astronomers face when attempting to find baby stars in the Milky Way?
output: Confounding the problem is all the dust standing between us and the center of our galaxy. Until now, nobody had been able to definitively locate any baby stars.

instruction: What does the discovery of young stars contribute to our understanding of star formation in different interstellar environments?
output: 'By studying individual stars in the galactic center, we can better understand how stars are formed in different interstellar environments,' said Deokkeun An of the Infrared Processing and Analysis Center at Caltech.

instruction: What future plans do astronomers have regarding the search for baby stars in the Milky Way?
output: The team plans to look for additional baby stars in the future, and ultimately to piece together what types of conditions allow stars to form in such an inhospitable environment as our galaxy's core.

instruction: What is the significance of the star's age in relation to planet formation?

instruction: What is the historical significance of the Yuba Goldfields in California?

instruction: What evidence do astronomers have regarding the collision of the Andromeda galaxy and the dwarf galaxy Messier 32?
output: Astronomers have new evidence that the Andromeda spiral galaxy was involved in a violent head-on collision with the neighboring dwarf galaxy Messier 32 (M32) more than 200 million years ago. instruction: What are the characteristics of the globular cluster Omega Centauri as observed by the Spitzer Space Telescope?
output: Millions of clustered stars glisten like an iridescent opal in a new image from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope. Called Omega Centauri, this sparkling orb of stars is like a miniature galaxy. It is the biggest and brightest of the more than 150 similar objects, called globular clusters, that orbit around the outside of our Milky Way galaxy. Stargazers at southern latitudes can spot the stellar gem with the naked eye in the constellation Centaurus.

instruction: What unique findings did the Spitzer Space Telescope reveal about the stars in Omega Centauri?
output: While the visible-light observations highlight the cluster's millions of jam-packed stars, Spitzer's infrared eyes reveal the dustier, more evolved stars tossed throughout the region. "Now we can see which stars form dust and can begin to understand how the dust forms and where it goes once it is expelled from a star," said Martha Boyer of the University of Minnesota, Twin Cities. Boyer is lead author of a paper about Omega Centauri appearing in the April issue of the Astronomical Journal. "Surprisingly, Spitzer revealed fewer of these dusty stars than expected."

instruction: What is the significance of the dust formed by stars in Omega Centauri?
output: As stars age and mature into red giants, they form dust grains, which play a vital role in the evolution of the universe and the formation of rocky planets," said Jacco van Loon, the study's principal investigator at Keele University in England. "Spitzer can see this dust, and it was able to resolve individual red giants even in the densest central parts of the cluster."

instruction: How old are the stars in Omega Centauri and what does their age imply about their formation?
output: Globular clusters are some of the oldest objects in our universe. Their stars are more than 12 billion years old, and, in most cases, formed all at once when the universe was just a toddler. Omega Centauri is unusual in that its stars are of different ages and possess varying levels of metals, or elements heavier than boron.

instruction: What does the presence of a medium-sized black hole in Omega Centauri suggest?
output: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope and Gemini Observatory on Cerro Pachon in Chile recently found evidence that Omega Centauri is home to a medium-sized black hole.

instruction: How does Spitzer's infrared imaging differ from visible-light observations in studying Omega Centauri?
output: While the visible-light observations highlight the cluster's millions of jam-packed stars, Spitzer's infrared eyes reveal the dustier, more evolved stars tossed throughout the region.

instruction: What is the role of the principal investigator Giovanni Fazio in the Spitzer mission?
output: Spitzer's infrared array camera, which took the Omega Centauri picture, was built by NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, Md. The instrument's principal investigator is Giovanni Fazio of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.

instruction: What key observation allows astronomers to understand the origin of Omega Centauri?
output: Astronomers say this points to a different origin for Omega Centauri than other globular clusters: they think it might be the core of a dwarf galaxy that was ripped apart and absorbed by our Milky Way long ago.

instruction: What instruments contributed to the imaging of the stars in Omega Centauri?
output: The stars colored blue are less evolved, like our own sun, and were captured by both Spitzer's infrared eyes and in visible light by the National Science Foundation's Blanco 4-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile.

instruction: What newly released image from the Spitzer Space Telescope shows the galaxy NGC 1291?
output: A newly released image from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope shows the galaxy NGC 1291. Though the galaxy is quite old, roughly 12 billion years, it is marked by an unusual ring where newborn stars are igniting.

instruction: What characterizes NGC 1291 as a barred galaxy?

instruction: What program is being conducted to analyze over 3,000 galaxies, including NGC 1291?
output: In a program called Spitzer Survey of Stellar Structure in Galaxies, or S4G, Sheth and his team of scientists are analyzing the structures of more than 3,000 galaxies in our local neighborhood.

instruction: How do bars of stars like those in NGC 1291 influence galaxy evolution?
output: The bars are a natural product of cosmic evolution, and they are part of the galaxies' endoskeleton. Examining this endoskeleton for the fossilized clues to their past gives us a unique view of their evolution.

instruction: What specific measurements can Spitzer make regarding the bar structures in galaxies?
output: Now, with Spitzer we can measure the precise shape and distribution of matter within the bar structures.

instruction: What effects do stellar bars have on gas distribution and star formation in galaxies?
output: When galaxies are young and gas-rich, stellar bars drive gas toward the center, feeding star formation. Over time, as the fuel runs out, the central regions become quiescent and star-formation activity shifts to the outskirts of a galaxy.

instruction: What ancient artifacts have been exposed by strong winds at Lake Colhué Huapi?
output: Los fuertes vientos que soplan a través del Lago Colhué Huapi han expuesto artefactos antiguos en medio del polvo de la superficie. Las tormentas de polvo son tan frecuentes y persistentes en esta zona que han expuesto un sitio arqueológico al aire libre a lo largo de la ribera del lago. El sitio Puesto Roberts 1, ubicado en una antigua llanura de inundación en el lado sureste del lago Colhué Huapi, fue identificado por primera vez en 2019, cuando los arqueólogos observaron que los vientos habían expuesto una capa de cinco centímetros de suelo franco arenoso llena de herramientas de piedra y los huesos de una especie de llama silvestre llamada guanaco.

instruction: What is the role of the MODIS instrument aboard NASA's Aqua satellite in studying dust activity at Lake Colhué Huapi?
output: El 29 de marzo de 2024, el espectrorradiómetro de imágenes de resolución moderada (MODIS, por sus siglas en inglés) a bordo del satélite Aqua de la NASA adquirió esta imagen de color natural del polvo que fluye desde el lecho limoso del lago, al este de lago Musters. El lago Colhué Huapi es una fuente de polvo particularmente rica porque el lago poco profundo crece y se encoge regularmente con las variaciones en el flujo del río Senguer y el ritmo de la evaporación.

instruction: How has the study of dust storms at Lake Colhué Huapi been conducted over the years?
output: Para comprender mejor la actividad del polvo del lago Colhué Huapi, los científicos de la NASA han analizado datos meteorológicos satelitales y de la superficie durante cinco décadas, evaluando la variabilidad anual de las tormentas de polvo e identificando los períodos de gran actividad. Las tormentas de polvo alcanzan su punto máximo durante el verano (de diciembre a marzo), aunque estos eventos también son comunes en invierno (de mayo a agosto).

instruction: What types of stone tools were found at the archaeological site Puesto Roberts 1?
output: Los arqueólogos identificaron 427 artefactos en este sitio —incluyendo cuchillas de corte hechas de piedra, herramientas de fresado, raspadores y boleadoras (bolas de piedra en forma de huevo utilizadas para la caza)— repartidos en un área de 15 metros cuadrados, según un estudio científico de 2022 dirigido por Heidi Hammond, arqueóloga de la Universidad Nacional de la Patagonia en San Juan Bosco.

instruction: What impact do the seasonal variations of the lake have on dust transport?
output: El lago Colhué Huapi es una fuente de polvo particularmente rica porque el lago poco profundo crece y se encoge regularmente con las variaciones en el flujo del río Senguer y el ritmo de la evaporación. Cuando los niveles de agua del lago son bajos, como cuando MODIS captó esta imagen, el viento transporta fácilmente partículas ligeras y de grano fino.

instruction: What findings were reported about the artifacts' material composition at Puesto Roberts 1?
output: La mayoría de las piedras estaban hechas de sílex, una roca sedimentaria de grano fino disponible en la localidad, pero los investigadores también encontraron muestras de cuarcita, andesita, basalto, xilópalo, riolita, obsidiana negra, toba, toba silicificada y artefactos de gneis.

instruction: What does the frequency of dust storms indicate about the environment around Lake Colhué Huapi?
output: En la mayoría de los años, ocurren de 15 a 30 tormentas de polvo de moderadas a grandes. Las tormentas de polvo son tan frecuentes y persistentes en esta zona que han expuesto un sitio arqueológico al aire libre a lo largo de la ribera del lago.

instruction: How does wind erosion affect the artifact sizes found at the archaeological site?
output: Al evaluar la distribución del tamaño de los artefactos, los artefactos más pequeños eran notablemente escasos. "Debido a la fuerte acción erosiva del viento", señalaron los autores, "este tipo de piezas probablemente se movilizaron y, por lo tanto, su representatividad en el ensamblaje es baja".

instruction: During which seasons do dust storms peak in the region of Lake Colhué Huapi?
output: Las tormentas de polvo alcanzan su punto máximo durante el verano (de diciembre a marzo), aunque estos eventos también son comunes en invierno (de mayo a agosto).

instruction: What is the significance of the Spitzer Space Telescope's observations of the Cigar Galaxy M82?

instruction: What significant chemical compounds were detected in the Spitzer spectra of protoplanetary discs?
output: In both infrared spectra, the presence of important chemicals for the formation of new worlds can be seen clearly. The broad depression in the center of each spectrum signifies the presence of silicates, which are chemically similar to beach sand. The depth of the silicate absorption feature indicates that the dusty cocoon surrounding the embedded protostar is extremely thick. Other absorption dips are produced by water ice (blue), methanol ice (red), and carbon dioxide ice (green).

instruction: How are crystalline silicates compared to the beaches of Hawaii in the context of protoplanetary discs?

instruction: What happens to the shape of a raindrop as it falls through the atmosphere?
output: As the raindrop falls, it loses that rounded shape. The raindrop becomes more like the top half of a hamburger bun. Flattened on the bottom and with a curved dome top, raindrops are anything but the classic tear shape. The reason is due to their speed falling through the atmosphere.

instruction: What role do dust and smoke particles play in the formation of raindrops?
output: High in the atmosphere, water collects on dust and smoke particles in clouds. Raindrops start to form in a roughly spherical structure due to the surface tension of water.

instruction: What causes surface tension in raindrops?
output: This surface tension is the "skin" of a body of water that makes the molecules stick together. The cause is the weak hydrogen bonds that occur between water molecules.

instruction: What occurs when raindrops collide while falling?
output: Even as a raindrop is falling, it will often collide with other raindrops and increase in size. Once the size of a raindrop gets too large, it will eventually break apart in the atmosphere back into smaller drops.

instruction: What is the maximum size a raindrop can reach before breaking apart?
output: Once the size of a raindrop gets too large, it will eventually break apart in the atmosphere back into smaller drops. This time, the surface tension loses and the large raindrop ceases to exist. Instead it pulls apart when it grows to around 4 millimeters or more.

instruction: How does airflow contribute to the shape of a raindrop?
output: Air flow on the bottom of the water drop is greater than the airflow at the top. At the top, small air circulation disturbances create less air pressure. The surface tension at the top allows the raindrop to remain more spherical while the bottom gets more flattened out.

instruction: What are the main factors affecting the shape and size of raindrops in precipitation?
output: The functional relationship between Zdr and Do is developed from the underlying microphysical relation between the mean axis ratio of raindrops and their size. This shape size relation can potentially be perturbed in the presence of raindrop oscillations.

instruction: What is the significance of the algorithms developed by Gorgucci et al. in precipitation measurement?
output: Gorgucci et al. (2001a,b) developed algorithms for retrieving rain rate (R) as well as Do, Nw and m using βe f f in combination with the measurement pair (Zh, Zdr).

instruction: What parameters of the drop size distribution can be retrieved from dual-polarization radar measurements?
output: Once Do is retrieved, then the other parameters of the DSD can be retrieved such as No of the normalized form of a Gamma distribution (Gorgucci et al., 2002).

instruction: What is Zdr and its significance in raindrop measurement?
output: Thus Zdr is a direct measure of mass weighted median diameter. The statistics of the parameter Do, Nw are important in the development of algorithms.

instruction: What does the infrared view of L1157 provided by NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope reveal about the formation of stars?
output: A rare, infrared view of a developing star and its flaring jets taken by NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope shows us what our own solar system might have looked like billions of years ago. In visible light, this star and its surrounding regions are completely hidden in darkness.

instruction: How do spinning clouds of gas and dust contribute to star formation?
output: Stars form out of spinning clouds, or envelopes, of gas and dust. As the envelopes flatten and collapse, jets of gas stream outward and a swirling disk of planet-forming material takes shape around the forming star. Eventually, the envelope and jets disappear, leaving a newborn star with a suite of planets. This process takes millions of years.

instruction: What is the significance of the DR21 region in the context of star formation?
output: Hidden behind a shroud of dust in the constellation Cygnus is an exceptionally bright source of radio emission called DR21. Visible light images reveal no trace of what is happening in this region because of heavy dust obscuration.

instruction: What does the Spitzer Space Telescope reveal about the star in the DR21 region?
output: This image, from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, allows us to peek behind the cosmic veil and pinpoint one of the most massive natal stars yet seen in our Milky Way galaxy. The never-before-seen star is 100,000 times as bright as the Sun.

instruction: Describe the structure and features observed in the 24-micron image mosaic from Spitzer's MIPS regarding DR21.
output: The image shows a 24-micron image mosaic, obtained with the Multiband Imaging Photometer aboard Spitzer (MIPS). This image maps the cooler infrared emission from interstellar dust found throughout the interstellar medium.

instruction: What unusual feature is observed in the 24-micron image mosaic of the DR21 region?
output: Perhaps the most fascinating feature in this image is a long and shadowy linear filament extending towards the 10 o'clock position of DR21. This jet of cold and dense gas, nearly 50 light-years in extent, appears in silhouette against a warmer background.

instruction: What may have caused the formation of the long filament observed in the Spitzer image?
output: This filament is too long and massive to be a stellar jet and may have formed from a pre-existing molecular cloud core sculpted by DR21's strong winds.

instruction: How does the Spitzer MIPS image contribute to understanding interstellar turbulence in the DR21 region?
output: Regardless of its true nature, this jet and the numerous other arcs and wisps of cool dust signify the interstellar turbulence normally unseen by the human eye.

instruction: What was the classification of the meteorite recovered at Sutter's Mill?
output: An international team of 70 researchers reported in the December 20 issue of the journal Science that this meteorite was classified as a Carbonaceous-Mighei (CM-type) carbonaceous chondrite and that they were able to identify for the first time the source region of these meteorites.

instruction: What instrument was used to detect the meteorites recovered at Sutter's Mill?
output: Detection of the falling meteorites by Doppler weather radar allowed for rapid recovery so that scientists could study for the first time a primitive meteorite with little exposure to the elements, providing the most pristine look yet at the surface of primitive asteroids.

instruction: What speed did the asteroid achieve when it impacted over California's Sierra Nevada?
output: The small three meter-sized asteroid that impacted over California's Sierra Nevada came in at twice the speed of typical meteorite falls. Clocked at 64,000 miles per hour, it was the biggest impact over land since the impact of the four-meter-sized asteroid 2008 TC3, four years ago over Sudan.

instruction: Which asteroid family was proposed as a source region for CM chondrites?
output: A good candidate source region for CM chondrites now is the Eulalia asteroid family, recently proposed as a source of primitive C-class asteroids in orbits that pass Earth.

instruction: What was a significant mineral detected in the meteorite and its implication?
output: Mike Zolensky, a mineralogist at NASA's Johnson Space Center, Houston, was surprised to detect the mineral oldhamite, a calcium sulfide, known in the past to disappear from contact with water by simply breathing on it. This mineral was known before mainly from rare enstatite chondrites, and its presence in the regolith breccia could mean that primitive and highly evolved asteroids collided with each other even at early times when the debris accumulated that now makes the meteorite matrix.

instruction: How many meteorites were recovered from the Sutter's Mill event?
output: Of the estimated 100,000-pound asteroid, less than 2 pounds was recovered on the ground in the form of 77 meteorites. The biggest was 205 grams.

instruction: What unique compound was detected in the meteorite that typically disappears quickly after landing?
output: The rapid recovery resulted in the detection of compounds that quickly disappear once a meteorite lands on Earth.

instruction: What were the reflective properties of the Sutter's Mill meteorite similar to?
output: In addition, Sutter's Mill has the same reflective properties as near-Earth asteroid, 1999 JU3, the mission target of the Hayabusa 2 sample return mission currently being prepared by the Japanese space agency, JAXA.

instruction: What percentage of the Sutter's Mill meteorite was actual gold?
output: Only 150 parts per billion of Sutter's Mill was actual gold, said co-author and cosmochemist Qing-zhu Yin of the University of California, Davis, but all of it was scientific gold.

instruction: What did the analysis of Sutter's Mill meteorite reveal about early Earth's carbon?
output: It is thought that the carbon atoms in our body may have been brought to Earth by such primitive asteroids in the early stages of our planet's history.

instruction: What is the significance of the Large Magellanic Cloud for astronomers studying star formation?
output: Astronomers are particularly interested in the LMC because its fractional content of heavy metals is two to five times lower than is seen in our solar neighborhood. In this context, 'heavy elements' refer to those elements not present in the primordial universe. Such elements as carbon, oxygen and others are produced by nucleosynthesis and are ejected into the interstellar medium via mass loss by stars, including supernova explosions. As such, the LMC provides a nearby cosmic laboratory that may resemble the distant universe in its chemical composition.

instruction: What are the features represented in the Spitzer image of Henize 206?

Blue represents invisible infrared light at wavelengths of 3.6 and 4.5 microns. Note that most of the stars in the field of view radiate primarily at these short infrared wavelengths. Cyan denotes emission at 5.8 microns, green depicts the 8.0 micron light, and red is used to trace the thermal emission from dust at 24 microns.

instruction: What initiated the new generation of star formation in Henize 206?

instruction: What historical events led to the control of St. Croix by different nations?

Starting in the 17th century, the island was successively claimed by the Spanish, the French, the French West India Company, and, for the next 200 years, the Danish West India Company. instruction: What happened to the pulsar 4U 0142+61 approximately 100,000 years ago?
output: The pulsar, called 4U 0142+61, was once a massive star until about 100,000 years ago when it blew up in a supernova explosion and scattered dusty debris into space.

instruction: What is the significance of the disk surrounding the pulsar 4U 0142+61?
output: Some of that debris was captured into what astronomers refer to as a "fallback disk," now circling the remaining stellar core, or pulsar. The disk resembles protoplanetary disks around young stars, out of which planets are thought to be born.

instruction: How do supernovas contribute to the formation of heavy metals in the universe?
output: Supernovas are a source of iron, nitrogen and other "heavy metals" in the universe. They spray these elements out into space, where they eventually come together in clouds that give rise to new stars and planets.

instruction: What discovery in 1992 suggested the possibility of planets forming around pulsars?

instruction: What insights have scientists gained regarding the eating habits of supermassive black holes from Spitzer Space Telescope data?
output: Data from NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope has given scientists new insights into why some supermassive black holes shine differently than others.

instruction: What phenomenon occurs as material falls into a supermassive black hole?
output: As supermassive black holes gobble up gas and dust, the material gets heated up just before it falls in, creating incredible light shows — sometimes brighter than an entire galaxy full of stars.

instruction: How do the black holes in the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies differ in their eating patterns?
output: The black holes at the center of the Milky Way (Earth's home galaxy) and Andromeda (one of our nearest galactic neighbors) are among the quietest eaters in the universe.

instruction: What method did researchers use to study the feeding behavior of Andromeda's supermassive black hole?
output: Using computer models, the authors simulated how gas and dust in proximity to Andromeda's supermassive black hole might behave over time.

instruction: What did the authors conclude about the spirals of dust identified by Spitzer in relation to Andromeda's supermassive black hole?
output: When the authors compared their findings to data from Spitzer and NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, they found spirals of dust previously identified by Spitzer that fit within these constraints. From this, the authors concluded that the spirals are feeding Andromeda's supermassive black hole.

instruction: What role does the disk of hot gas play in the feeding of a supermassive black hole?
output: The simulation demonstrated that a small disk of hot gas could form close to the supermassive black hole and feed it continuously.

instruction: What are the implications of the findings on the brightness of supermassive black holes?
output: The brightness of the black hole fluctuates when the material is consumed in clumps of different sizes.

instruction: How did Spitzer Space Telescope's observations contribute to our understanding of Andromeda's structure?
output: By separating these wavelengths and looking at the dust alone, astronomers can see the galaxy's 'skeleton' — places where gas has coalesced and cooled, sometimes forming dust, creating conditions for stars to form.

instruction: What surprises did Spitzer's view of Andromeda reveal regarding its structure?
output: Although it is a spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, Andromeda is dominated by a large dust ring rather than distinct arms circling its center.

instruction: What challenges did Spitzer face when imaging the Andromeda galaxy?
output: Even with a field of view wider than Hubble's, Spitzer had to take 11,000 snapshots to create this comprehensive picture of Andromeda.

instruction: What analogy is used to describe how gas approaches the supermassive black hole?

instruction: What is the detailed chemical fingerprint of Gliese 3470 b as revealed by Hubble and Spitzer?
output: Two NASA space telescopes have teamed up to identify, for the first time, the detailed chemical "fingerprint" of a planet between the sizes of Earth and Neptune. No planets like this can be found in our own solar system, but they are common around other stars.

instruction: How does Gliese 3470 b compare to other planets in terms of mass?
output: The planet, Gliese 3470 b (also known as GJ 3470 b), may be a cross between Earth and Neptune, with a large rocky core buried under a deep, crushing hydrogen-and-helium atmosphere. Weighing in at 12.6 Earth masses, the planet is more massive than Earth but less massive than Neptune (which is more than 17 Earth masses).

instruction: What method is used to analyze the chemical fingerprints of GJ 3470 b's atmosphere?
output: By inventorying the contents of GJ 3470 b's atmosphere, astronomers are able to uncover clues about the planet's nature and origin. The science of analyzing chemical fingerprints based on light is called "spectroscopy."

instruction: What surprising elements were found in the atmosphere of GJ 3470 b?
output: We expected an atmosphere strongly enriched in heavier elements like oxygen and carbon which are forming abundant water vapor and methane gas, similar to what we see on Neptune. Instead, we found an atmosphere that is so poor in heavy elements that its composition resembles the hydrogen/helium-rich composition of the Sun.

instruction: What was the formation hypothesis for Gliese 3470 b according to Björn Benneke?
output: The most plausible explanation, according to Benneke, is that GJ 3470 b was born precariously close to its red dwarf star, which is about half the mass of our Sun. He hypothesizes that essentially it started out as a dry rock and rapidly accreted hydrogen from a primordial disk of gas when its star was very young.

instruction: How do transits and eclipses contribute to the observation of GJ 3470 b?
output: This was accomplished by measuring the absorption of starlight as the planet passed in front of its star (transit) and the loss of reflected light from the planet as it passed behind the star (eclipse). All told, the space telescopes observed 12 transits and 20 eclipses.

instruction: What conclusion does Benneke draw about the atmosphere of GJ 3470 b?
output: For the first time we have a spectroscopic signature of such a world. Fortuitously, the atmosphere of GJ 3470 b turned out to be mostly clear, with only thin hazes, enabling the scientists to probe deep into the atmosphere.

instruction: What new capabilities will the James Webb Space Telescope provide for studying GJ 3470 b?
output: NASA's upcoming James Webb Space Telescope will be able to probe even deeper into GJ 3470 b's atmosphere, thanks to Webb's unprecedented sensitivity in the infrared.

instruction: What makes the atmosphere of GJ 3470 b unique compared to traditional models of planet formation?
output: Other exoplanets, called "hot Jupiters," are thought to form far from their stars and over time migrate much closer. But this planet seems to have formed just where it is today, said Benneke.

instruction: What are the implications of the discovery of GJ 3470 b for understanding planets in our galaxy?
output: Many similar worlds have been discovered by NASA's Kepler space observatory, whose mission ended in 2018. In fact, 80% of the planets in our galaxy may fall into this mass range.

instruction: What is the significance of the discovery of the planet OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb?
output: Scientists have discovered a new planet with the mass of Earth, orbiting its star at the same distance that we orbit our sun. The planet is likely far too cold to be habitable for life as we know it, however, because its star is so faint. But the discovery adds to scientists' understanding of the types of planetary systems that exist beyond our own.

instruction: What technique was used to discover OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb?
output: Microlensing is a technique that facilitates the discovery of distant objects by using background stars as flashlights. When a star crosses precisely in front of a bright star in the background, the gravity of the foreground star focuses the light of the background star, making it appear brighter. A planet orbiting the foreground object may cause an additional blip in the star's brightness. In this case, the blip only lasted a few hours.

instruction: What data sources were used to detect OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb?
output: For the new study, researchers were alerted to the initial microlensing event by the ground-based Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) survey, managed by the University of Warsaw in Poland. Study authors used the Korea Microlensing Telescope Network (KMTNet), operated by the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute, and Spitzer, to track the event from Earth and space.

instruction: What observations did scientists make from KMTNet regarding the new planet?
output: With both KMTNet and Spitzer observing the event, scientists had two vantage points from which to study the objects involved, as though two eyes separated by a great distance were viewing it. Having data from these two perspectives allowed them to detect the planet with KMTNet and calculate the mass of the star and the planet using Spitzer data.

instruction: Why is OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb considered to have a low habitability potential?
output: Although OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb is about the same mass as Earth, and the same distance from its host star as our planet is from our sun, the similarities may end there. OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb is nearly 13,000 light-years away and orbits a star so small, scientists aren't sure if it's a star at all. It could be a brown dwarf, a star-like object whose core is not hot enough to generate energy through nuclear fusion.

instruction: How does the distribution of planets in the Milky Way's bulge compare to its disk according to the researchers?
output: An open question is whether there is a difference in the frequency of planets in the Milky Way's central bulge compared to its disk, the pancake-like region surrounding the bulge. OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb is located in the disk, as are two planets previously detected through microlensing by NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope. The lack of Spitzer detections in the bulge suggests that planets may be less common toward the center of our galaxy than in the disk.

instruction: What did NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter reveal about martian glaciers?

instruction: What was the significance of the buried glaciers discovered on Mars?
