instruction: Describe el fenómeno de los agujeros negros y su formación.
output: Un agujero negro es un objeto astronómico con una fuerza gravitatoria tan fuerte que nada, ni siquiera la luz, puede escapar de él. La "superficie" de un agujero negro, denominada horizonte de sucesos, define el límite donde la velocidad requerida para evadirlo excede la velocidad de la luz, que es el límite de velocidad en el cosmos. La materia y la radiación son atrapadas y no pueden salir.

instruction: ¿Cuáles son las dos clases principales de agujeros negros y cómo se diferencian?
output: Se han estudiado extensivamente dos clases principales de agujeros negros. Los agujeros negros de masa estelar, de tres a docenas de veces la masa del Sol, se extienden por toda nuestra galaxia, la Vía Láctea, mientras que los monstruos supermasivos que pesan entre 100.000 a milles de millones de masas solares se encuentran en los centros de la mayoría de las galaxias grandes, incluida la nuestra.

instruction: ¿Qué evento llevó a la identificación más concreta de un agujero negro de masa intermedia?
output: Mientras un puñado de candidatos han sido identificados por evidencia indirecta, el ejemplo más concreto hasta la fecha se observó el 21 de mayo de 2019, cuando el Observatorio de ondas gravitatorias por interferometría láser (LIGO, por sus siglas en inglés) de la Fundación Nacional de Ciencias de Estados Unidos, ubicada en Livingston, Luisiana y Hanford, Washington, detectó las ondas gravitacionales de una fusión entre dos agujeros negros de masa estelar. Este evento, denominado GW190521, creó un agujero negro que pesaba 142 soles.

instruction: ¿Cómo se forman los agujeros negros de masa estelar?
output: Un agujero negro de masa estelar se forma cuando una estrella de más de 20 masas solares agota el combustible en su núcleo y colapsa bajo su propio peso. El colapso desencadena la explosión de una supernova que expulsa las capas exteriores de la estrella. Pero si el núcleo aplastado contiene más de tres veces la masa del Sol, ninguna fuerza podrá detener su colapso en un agujero negro.

instruction: Describe el primer avistamiento de un agujero negro utilizando el Telescopio de Horizonte de Sucesos.
output: En 2019, astrónomos captaron la primera imagen de un agujero negro utilizando el Telescopio de Horizonte de Sucesos (EHT, por sus siglas en inglés), en una colaboración internacional que conectó a ocho radiotelescopios terrestres bajo una sola antena del tamaño de la Tierra. En la imagen aparece como un círculo oscuro delimitado por un disco en órbita de materia caliente y brillante. El agujero negro supermasivo se encuentra en el corazón de una galaxia llamada M87, ubicada a unos 55 millones de años luz de distancia, y pesa más de 6 miles de millones de masas solares.

instruction: ¿Qué impacto tuvo la detección de ondas gravitacionales en el estudio de los agujeros negros?
output: Otro hito importante en el estudio de los agujeros negros se dio en 2015 cuando los científicos detectaron por primera vez las ondas gravitacionales, las mismas ondas del tejido del espacio-tiempo que un siglo antes había predicho Albert Einstein, en su teoría general de la relatividad. LIGO detectó las ondas de un evento ocurrido hace 1.300 millones de años, conocido como GW150914, en el que dos agujeros negros giraban entre sí, en espiral, mientras se fusionaban.

instruction: Menciona los telescopios que continúan observando agujeros negros y sus entornos.
output: Los telescopios espaciales de la NASA Hubble, Chandra, Swift, NuSTAR y NICER, así como los instrumentos de otras misiones, continúan observando los agujeros negros y sus entornos para que podamos aprender más sobre estos enigmáticos objetos y su papel en la evolución de las galaxias y del universo.

instruction: ¿Cómo se sienten las ondas gravitacionales en la cercanía de un agujero negro?
output: Aunque la luz no puede escapar del horizonte de eventos de un agujero negro, las enormes ondas gravitacionales en sus cercanías hacen que la materia cercana se caliente millones de grados y emita ondas de radio y rayos X.

instruction: ¿Qué son los chorros de materia generados por agujeros negros supermasivos?
output: Parte de la materia que orbita aún más cerca del horizonte de eventos pueden ser expedida, formando chorros de partículas que se mueven cercanas a la velocidad de la luz emitiendo ondas de radio, rayos X y rayos gamma. Los chorros de materia de los agujeros negros supermasivos se pueden extender cientos de miles de años luz.

instruction: What was the primary mission objective of the Earth Observing-1 (EO-1) satellite?

instruction: What technological advancement does the Advanced Land Imager (ALI) sensor represent?
output: The Advanced Land Imager (ALI) sensor demonstrates a potential technological direction for the next generation of Landsat sensors.

instruction: What are the benefits of comparing the ALI sensor capabilities to the Landsat 7 ETM+ and Terra MODIS sensors?

instruction: How were the measured TOA reflectances for ALI calibrated against ETM+ and MODIS?
output: The cross-calibration of ALI with ETM+ and MODIS was performed using near-simultaneous surface observations based on image statistics from areas observed by these sensors over four desert sites (Libya 4, Mauritania 2, Arabia 1, and Sudan 1).

instruction: What method was used to compensate for differences in the relative spectral response (RSR) when observing the same target?
output: The differences in the measured TOA reflectances due to RSR mismatches were compensated by using a spectral band adjustment factor (SBAF), which takes into account the spectral profile of the target and the RSR of each sensor.

instruction: What is the significance of the spectral profile of the target in this study?

instruction: What were the results of the TOA reflectance measurements for ALI after applying SBAF?

instruction: What is the primary purpose of the SWIRP instrument developed by NASA?
output: A new instrument is expected to give researchers unprecedented insights into the ice crystals that form the wispy clouds that float high in the sky and play an important, but little-understood role in Earth's climate.

instruction: How does the SWIRP instrument differ from the IceCube instrument?
output: SWIRP follows another instrument, also led by Wu, called IceCube. During its 15-month sojourn aboard a 3U CubeSat, IceCube produced the world's first map of the global distribution of atmospheric ice. It obtained this data in only one frequency band — 883-Gigahertz — while SWIRP will study the same phenomenon in multiple frequencies, ranging from the submillimeter or microwaves that fall between radio and longwave infrared on the electromagnetic spectrum.

instruction: What wavelengths does the SWIRP instrument measure ice clouds in?
output: SWIRP would allow scientists to see ice clouds more clearly because it measures ice clouds in three different wavelengths — the 680-Gigahertz, 240-Gigahertz and infrared bands — which are sensitive to differently sized particles.

instruction: What role do ice clouds play in Earth's climate according to the text?
output: Understanding ice clouds is important for interpreting Earth's radiation budget. Clouds determine how much sunlight gets in and how much gets bounced back into space. Clouds that sit at a lower altitude tend to reflect sunlight, while colder, higher-altitude clouds let more sunlight in and create a greenhouse effect.

instruction: What is a major challenge scientists face when studying cirrus clouds?
output: Scientists struggle to understand the impact of cirrus clouds because it's difficult to calculate how their plentiful and irregularly shaped ice crystals scatter sunlight.

instruction: What potential benefit does SWIRP provide in terms of NASA's observational capabilities?
output: Although existing sensors can observe small and very large ice particles, SWIRP can see intermediate ice particles, which closes an existing gap in NASA's observational capabilities.

instruction: How does SWIRP contribute to international cloud-ice observation efforts?
output: SWIRP will also enhance the international capabilities of cloud-ice observations. The Ice Cloud Imager, or ICI, now being developed by the European Organization for Meteorological Satellites, is a millimeter/submillimeter wave radiometer that will also measure ice clouds to support long-term climate monitoring and validate the characteristics of ice clouds in weather and climate models.

instruction: What advantages does SWIRP have over larger instruments like the Ice Cloud Imager?
output: Not only could it be built for less money, SWIRP would enable multi-point cloud observations from a constellation of SmallSats, which would provide complete daily coverage.

instruction: What is the funding source for the SWIRP project?
output: NASA's Earth Science Technology Office is funding this effort.

instruction: What future plans exist for the SWIRP instrument after its demonstration?
output: Once proven, the shoebox-sized instrument would be ready to fly on a satellite mission, Wu said.

instruction: What was the objective of the research conducted by Turner et al. in assessing satellite observing configurations?

instruction: What are the limitations of satellite observations of atmospheric methane columns?
output: Satellite observations of atmospheric methane columns are an attractive approach for monitoring these emissions but have limitations from instrument precision, pixel resolution, and measurement frequency.

instruction: What configurations were evaluated in the observation system simulation experiment (OSSE) related to methane emissions?
output: We present an observation system simulation experiment (OSSE) to assess the capabilities of different satellite observing system configurations.

instruction: What spatial resolution was achieved in the WRF-STILT simulation for methane column footprints?
output: We conduct a 1-week WRF-STILT simulation to generate methane column footprints at 1.3 × 1.3 km2 spatial resolution.

instruction: How often is the TROPOMI instrument able to take measurements of methane emissions?
output: The observing characteristics of the recently launched TROPOMI instrument (7 × 7 km2 pixels, 11 ppb precision, daily frequency).

instruction: What resolution should TROPOMI observations provide information on temporally invariant emissions?
output: We find that a week of TROPOMI observations should provide information on temporally invariant emissions at ∼ 30 km spatial resolution.

instruction: What is the precision requirement for GeoCARB to achieve fine resolution of methane emissions?
output: A precision better than 6 ppb is critical for GeoCARB to achieve fine resolution of emissions.

instruction: What type of emissions would be missed by both TROPOMI and GeoCARB instruments?
output: Transient emissions would be missed with either TROPOMI or GeoCARB.

instruction: What are the expected advantages of a high-resolution geostationary instrument for monitoring methane emissions?
output: An aspirational highresolution geostationary instrument with 1.3 × 1.3 km2 pixel resolution, hourly return time, and 1 ppb precision would effectively constrain the temporally invariant emissions in the Barnett Shale at the kilometer scale and provide some information on hourly variability of sources.

instruction: What is the spatial resolution of the GeoCARB instrument and its relation to sampling frequency?
output: GeoCARB should provide information available on temporally invariant emissions ∼ 2-7 km spatial resolution depending on sampling frequency (hourly to daily).

instruction: What observations did the Spitzer Space Telescope make regarding the planets' temperatures and orbits?

instruction: How do visible light and infrared views differ in the representation of a star and its planet?

instruction: What is the primary improvement of the new algorithm for MODIS satellite retrievals of aerosol optical thickness discussed in the 2010 publication by Wang et al.?
output: A new algorithm, using the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite reflectance and aerosol single scattering properties simulated from a chemistry transport model (GEOS-Chem), is developed to retrieve aerosol optical thickness (AOT) over land in China during the spring dust season. The algorithm first uses a "dynamic lower envelope" approach to sample the MODIS dark-pixel reflectance data in low AOT conditions, to derive the local surface visible (0.65 μm)/near infrared (NIR, 2.1 μm) reflectance ratio.

instruction: How does the new algorithm improve the accuracy of aerosol optical thickness retrievals compared to the MODIS Collection 5 AOT algorithm?
output: Comparison of retrieved AOT results in April and May of 2008 with AERONET observations shows a strong correlation (R = 0.83), with small bias (0.01), and small RMSE (0.17); the figures are a substantial improvement over corresponding values obtained with the MODIS Collection 5 AOT algorithm for the same study region and time period.

instruction: What is the role of the linearized vector radiative transfer model (VLIDORT) in the new algorithm for aerosol optical thickness retrieval?
output: A linearized vector radiative transfer model (VLIDORT) that simultaneously computes the top-of-atmosphere reflectance and its Jacobian with respect to AOT, is used in the forward component of the inversion of MODIS reflectance to AOT.

instruction: What are the implications of the improved AOT retrieval for air quality monitoring in China?

instruction: What correlation and RMSE values were found when comparing the retrieved AOT results with AERONET observations?

instruction: How do the retrieved concentrations of surface PM10 derived from the new AOT retrieval compare to ground observations?

instruction: What is the average global-mean all-sky instantaneous top-of-the-atmosphere forcing induced by quadrupling CO2?

instruction: What is the fully adjusted radiative forcing mean value after accounting for adjustments?

instruction: What contributes significantly to the intermodel spread of surface temperature projections?

instruction: What is the primary reason for the Maunder Minimum cooling relative to today?
output: The results showed that 1) the Maunder Minimum cooling relative to today was primarily associated with reduced anthropogenic radiative forcing, although the solar reduction added 40% to the overall cooling.

instruction: What impact did the solar irradiance have on the climate during the Maunder Minimum?

instruction: What was the global surface temperature change when using different irradiance prescriptions?
output: The global surface temperature change was similar when using the total and spectral irradiance prescriptions, although the tropical response was somewhat greater with the former, and the stratospheric response greater with the latter.

instruction: How did the stratospheric ozone respond to changes in atmospheric composition during the Maunder Minimum?
output: Stratospheric ozone was most affected by the difference between present-day and preindustrial atmospheric composition and chemistry, with increases in the upper and lower stratosphere during the Maunder Minimum.

instruction: What role did anthropogenic effects play in stratospheric ozone changes during the Maunder Minimum?
output: While the estimated UV reduction led to ozone decreases, this was generally less important than the anthropogenic effect except in the upper midstratosphere, as judged by two different ozone photochemistry schemes.

instruction: What were the key characteristics of the North Atlantic Oscillation during the Maunder Minimum?
output: Most experiments produce a relative negative phase of the North Atlantic Oscillation/Arctic Oscillation (NAO/AO) during the Maunder Minimum, with both solar and anthropogenic forcing equally capable, associated with the tropical cooling and relative poleward Eliassen-Palm (EP) flux refraction.

instruction: What was the significance of using a full stratosphere in climate models for the Maunder Minimum?
output: A full stratosphere appeared to be necessary for the negative AO/NAO phase, as was the case with this model for global warming experiments, unless the cooling was very large, while the ozone response played a minor role and did not influence surface temperature significantly.

instruction: What is the model sensitivity used in the simulations referenced in the study?
output: The global and tropical response was greater than 1ЊC, in a model with a sensitivity of 1.2ЊC (W m Ϫ2 )Ϫ1. To reproduce recent low-end estimates would require a sensitivity one-fourth as large.

instruction: What models were used for simulating climate during the Maunder Minimum?

instruction: What is the purpose of the experiments conducted in the study?
output: Experiments were made to investigate the effect of total versus spectrally varying solar irradiance changes; spectrally varying solar irradiance changes on the stratospheric ozone/climate response with both preindustrial and present trace gases; and the impact on climate and stratospheric ozone of the preindustrial trace gases and aerosols by themselves.

instruction: What are the main functions of the POLRADS instrument?
output: To obtain the polarized in-water upwelling spectral radiance distribution data we have developed the POLRADS instrument. This instrument is based on the NuRADS radiance distribution camera systems in which linear polarizer's have been installed. By combining simultaneous images from three NuRADS instruments, three Stokes parameters (I, Q, U) for the water leaving radiance can be obtained for all upwelling angles simultaneously.

instruction: What uncertainties are associated with the measurements from POLRADS?
output: This system measures the Stokes parameters Q/I and U/I with a 0.05-0.06 uncertainty and I with a 7-10% uncertainty.

instruction: Which research program is the POLRADS instrument part of?

instruction: What is the expected increase in burned area due to wildfires in boreal North America over the next 50-100 years?

instruction: How much smaller were median cloud droplet radii in smoky clouds compared to background clouds?

instruction: What is the calculated value of aerosol-cloud interactions (ACI) based on the relationship between cloud droplet number and biomass burning tracers?
output: Based on the relationship between cloud droplet number (Nliq ) and various biomass burning tracers (BBt ) across the multi-campaign data set, we calculated the magnitude of subarctic and Arctic smoke aerosol-cloud interactions (ACIs, where ACI = (1/3) × d ln(Nliq )/d ln(BBt )) to be ∼ 0.16 out of a maximum possible value of 0.33 that would be obtained if all aerosols were to nucleate cloud droplets.

instruction: What was the ACI value found in a subarctic case study with low liquid water content?

instruction: How much could the smoke-driven cloud albedo effect decrease local summertime short-wave radiative flux in the subarctic?
output: Using our calculated ACI values, we estimate that the smoke-driven cloud albedo effect may decrease local summertime short-wave radiative flux by between 2 and 4 W m−2 or more under some low and homogeneous cloud cover conditions in the subarctic, although the changes should be smaller in high surface albedo regions of the Arctic.

instruction: What is the impact of high concentrations of cloud condensation nuclei on droplet formation in polluted clouds?

instruction: What is the dominant habitat type for cyanobacterial communities in the Atacama Desert?
output: Cyanobacterial communities at all sites are predominantly (!75%) ‘perilithic' (confined to the periphery of rocks) and occur in non-random spatial patterns (‘‘island patches'') at multiple scales.

instruction: What geographic coordinates were used for the Aguas Calientes study site in the Atacama Desert?
output: A high resolution mapping of a single 18-m2 rock cluster at the Aguas Calientes study site (25°S, 69°W) revealed colonization of 5.2% (49 of 948 quartz rocks) and showed colonized rocks to be much larger (~2X) than the available mean rock size.

instruction: What methods were used to analyze the spatial distribution of cyanobacterial patches?
output: Ripley's K and point pattern analyses show that quartz rocks are not ‘‘selected'' or occupied by cyanobacteria randomly, but that non-random processes distinct from those creating the background rock pattern must be invoked to explain microbial patchiness in the Atacama Desert.

instruction: What physical controls affect the microbial patchiness of cyanobacterial communities in the Atacama Desert?

instruction: What unique pattern do cyanobacterial patches exhibit in the Atacama Desert?

instruction: What are the primary scientific objectives of the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS)?
output: The Atmospheric Infrared Sounder, AIRS, in conjunction with the Advanced Microwave Sounding Unit, AMSU, sense emitted infrared and microwave radiation from the Earth to provide a three-dimensional look at Earth's weather and climate. Working in tandem, the two instruments make simultaneous observations all the way down to the Earth's surface, even in the presence of heavy clouds. With more than 2,000 channels sensing different regions of the atmosphere, the system creates a global, 3-dimensional map of atmospheric temperature and humidity, cloud amounts and heights, greenhouse gas concentrations, and many other atmospheric phenomena.

instruction: What effects do clouds over snow and ice have on ozone absorption according to the study?
output: In this paper, we examine how clouds over snow and ice affect ozone absorption and how these effects may be accounted for in satellite retrieval algorithms. Over snow and ice, the Aura Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) Raman cloud pressure algorithm derives an effective scene pressure.

instruction: What is the threshold pressure difference used to detect clouds that shield tropospheric ozone absorption?
output: A pressure difference of 100 hPa is used as a crude threshold for the detection of clouds that significantly shield tropospheric ozone absorption.

instruction: How do the OMI effective scene pressure and MODIS cloud top pressure work together in cloud analysis?
output: Combining the OMI effective scene pressure and the Aqua MODerate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) cloud top pressure, we can distinguish between shielding and non-shielding clouds.

instruction: What factors influence the amount of shielding provided by clouds over a bright surface?
output: The amount of shielding provided by clouds depends upon the geometry (solar and satellite zenith angles) and the surface albedo as well as cloud optical thickness.

instruction: What error does the current TOMS total column ozone algorithm assume when applied to snow and ice?
output: The current Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer (TOMS) total column ozone algorithm (that has also been applied to the OMI) assumes no clouds over snow and ice. This assumption leads to errors in the retrieved ozone column.

instruction: How does using OMI effective scene pressures over snow and ice affect the spatial distribution of retrieved total ozone?
output: We show that the use of OMI effective scene pressures over snow and ice reduces these errors and leads to a more homogeneous spatial distribution of the retrieved total ozone.

instruction: What observations were used to qualitatively evaluate the study's approach on cloud shielding?
output: We also use CloudSat observations to qualitatively evaluate our approach.

instruction: What is the significance of radiative transfer simulations performed in the study?
output: To evaluate this approach, we performed radiative transfer simulations under various observing conditions.

instruction: Which satellites operate together in the A-train constellation mentioned in the study?
output: The CloudSat, Aqua, and Aura satellites fly in an afternoon polar orbit constellation with ground overpass times within 15 min of each other.

instruction: What results indicate the sensitivity of top-of-the-atmosphere radiance to ozone absorption related to cloud coverage?
output: Using cloud vertical extinction profiles from the CloudSat Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR), we find that clouds over a bright surface can produce significant shielding (i.e., a reduction in the sensitivity of the top-of-the-atmosphere radiance to ozone absorption below the clouds).

instruction: What is the purpose of the variable localization method in the ensemble Kalman filter for carbon cycle data assimilation?
output: We introduce a "variable localization" method, zeroing out such covariances between unrelated variables to the problem of assimilating carbon dioxide concentrations into a dynamical model using the local ensemble transform Kalman filter (LETKF) in an observing system simulation experiments (OSSE) framework.

instruction: How does variable localization affect the error covariance estimates in the ensemble Kalman filter?
output: Such variable localization scheme zeroes out the background error covariance among prognostic variables that are not physically related, thus reducing sampling errors.

instruction: What improvement does the variable localization method achieve compared to the standard full covariance approach?
output: Results from the identical twin experiments show that the performance in the estimation of surface carbon fluxes obtained using variable localization is much better than that using a standard full covariance approach.

instruction: What is the relationship between carbon variables and wind field in the context of the local ensemble transform Kalman filter?
output: With emphasis on configurations allowing nonzero error covariance between carbon variables and the wind field, which affects transport of atmospheric CO2, but not between CO2 and the other meteorological variables.

instruction: What were the findings regarding surface carbon flux estimation when applying variable localization over time?
output: The relative improvement increases when the surface fluxes change with time and model error becomes significant.

instruction: In what framework is the variable localization method applied for the carbon cycle data assimilation?
output: Using the local ensemble transform Kalman filter (LETKF) in an observing system simulation experiments (OSSE) framework.

instruction: Who are the authors of the publication on variable localization in an ensemble Kalman filter?
output: Kang, J. , E. Kalnay , J. Liu , I. Fung , T. Miyoshi, and K. Ide (2011), "Variable localization" in an ensemble Kalman filter: Application to the carbon cycle data assimilation.

instruction: What is the significance of the term 'sampling errors' in the context of ensemble Kalman filters?
output: When two variables are not physically correlated, their error covariance is still estimated by the ensemble and, therefore, it is dominated by sampling errors.

instruction: What methods are explored for the LETKF concerning the carbon cycle data assimilation?
output: A range of covariance structures are explored for the LETKF, with emphasis on configurations allowing nonzero error covariance between carbon variables and the wind field.

instruction: What is the main focus of the research conducted by Kang et al. in their publication?
output: The main focus is on the 'variable localization' method in the ensemble Kalman filter and its application to carbon cycle data assimilation.

instruction: What was the percentage enhancement of emissions due to traffic congestion measured in the study?

instruction: What model is used to diagnose the mechanisms producing the water vapor seasonal cycle in the tropical tropopause layer?
output: We use a forward Lagrangian trajectory model to diagnose mechanisms that produce the water vapor seasonal cycle observed by the Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) and reproduced by the Goddard Earth Observing System Chemistry-Climate Model (GEOSCCM) in the tropical tropopause layer (TTL).

instruction: How does the seasonal cycle of temperature affect water vapor in the tropical tropopause layer according to the study?

instruction: What is the impact of convective ice evaporation on the seasonal cycle of water vapor in the tropical tropopause layer?

instruction: In which latitude range is the seasonal cycle of water vapor found to be smaller than observed?

instruction: What contribution does convective ice evaporation make to the moistening of the tropical tropopause layer?

instruction: What is the primary influence of sea ice on global climate?
output: Even though sea ice occurs primarily in the polar regions, it influences our global climate. Sea ice has a bright surface, so much of the sunlight that strikes it is reflected back into space. As a result, areas covered by sea ice don't absorb much solar energy, so temperatures in the polar regions remain relatively cool.

instruction: What chain of events does the melting of sea ice start?
output: If gradually warming temperatures melt sea ice over time, fewer bright surfaces are available to reflect sunlight back into space, more solar energy is absorbed at the surface, and temperatures rise further. This chain of events starts a cycle of warming and melting.

instruction: How do the dark days of polar winter affect sea ice melting?
output: This cycle is temporarily halted when the dark days of the polar winter return, but it starts again in the following spring.

instruction: What makes polar regions sensitive to climate change?
output: Even a small increase in temperature can lead to greater warming over time, making the polar regions the most sensitive areas to climate change on Earth.

instruction: What is the goal of the study on multi-angle photo-polarimetry regarding aerosols?

instruction: What are the causes of large retrieval errors in XCO2 over deserts according to Zhang et al. (2016)?
output: Large retrieval errors in column-weighted CO2 mixing ratio (XCO2) over deserts are evident in the Orbiting Carbon Observatory 2 version 7 L2 products. We argue that these errors are caused by the surface albedo being close to a critical surface albedo (αc). Over a surface with albedo close to αc, increasing the aerosol optical depth (AOD) does not change the continuum radiance. The spectral signature caused by changing the AOD is identical to that caused by changing the absorbing gas column. The degeneracy in the retrievals of AOD and XCO2 results in a loss of degrees of freedom and information content.

instruction: What is the recommended approach to improve XCO2 retrieval accuracy under aerosol loading conditions?
output: We recommend a bias correction approach that has significantly improved the XCO2 retrieval from the California Laboratory for Atmospheric Remote Sensing data in the presence of aerosol loading.

instruction: How does the surface albedo affect the retrieval of XCO2 over deserts?
output: Over a surface with albedo close to αc, increasing the aerosol optical depth (AOD) does not change the continuum radiance. The degeneracy in the retrievals of AOD and XCO2 results in a loss of degrees of freedom and information content.

instruction: What model is used to study the physical mechanism of XCO2 retrieval error according to the publication?

instruction: What instruments were used to study the planet LP 791-18 d?

instruction: What are the potential implications of volcanic activity on LP 791-18 d for its atmosphere?

instruction: What is the relevance of the gravitational interactions between planets c and d in the system?

instruction: What is the impact of aerosols on the cloud radiative effect of marine stratocumulus clouds?
output: Marine stratocumulus clouds (MSC) cover large areas over the oceans and possess super sensitivity of their cloud radiative effect to changes in aerosol concentrations. Aerosols can cause transitions between regimes of fully cloudy closed cells and open cells. The possible role of aerosols in cloud cover has a big impact on the amount of reflected solar radiation from the clouds, thus potentially constitutes very large aerosol indirect radiative effect, which can exceed 100 Wm-2.

instruction: How do anthropogenic aerosols affect the lifespan of closed marine stratocumulus clouds?
output: It is hypothesized that continentally polluted clouds remain in closed cells regime for longer time from leaving continent and hence for longer distance away from land, thus occupying larger ocean areas with full cloud cover. Attributing this to anthropogenic aerosols would imply a very large negative radiative forcing with a significant climate impact.

instruction: What observations were used to analyze the closed cell formation over the northeast Atlantic Ocean?
output: This possibility is confirmed by analyzing a detailed case study based on geostationary and polar-orbiting satellite observations of the microphysical and dynamical evolution of MSC. We show that large area of closed cells was formed over the northeast Atlantic Ocean downwind of Europe in a continentally polluted air mass.

instruction: What process was tracked during the cleansing of the closed marine stratocumulus clouds?
output: The closed cells undergo cleansing process that was tracked for 3.5 days that resulted with a rapid transition from closed to open cells once the clouds started drizzling heavily.

instruction: What term is used to describe the process of cloud breakup due to meteorological and aerosol considerations?
output: The mechanism leading to the eventual breakup of the clouds due to both meteorological and aerosol considerations is elucidated. We termed this cleansing and cloud breakup process maritimization.

instruction: What is the climatological significance of the situations described in the study?
output: Further study is needed to assess the climatological significance of such situations.

instruction: What larger variation in ultraviolet does the solar spectral irradiance suggest according to the SORCE measurements?
output: The 11-yr solar cycle in solar spectral irradiance (SSI) inferred from measurements by the SOlar Radiation & Climate Experiment (SORCE) suggests a much larger variation in the ultraviolet than previously accepted.

instruction: How does the GEOSCCM model simulate ozone response to solar cycles using different SSI descriptions?
output: We present middle atmosphere ozone and temperature responses to the solar cycles in SORCE SSI and the ubiquitous Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) SSI reconstruction using the Goddard Earth Observing System chemistry-climate model (GEOSCCM).

instruction: What is the difference in modeled ozone response between SORCE SSI and NRL SSI in the stratosphere?
output: The modeled ozone response is positive throughout the stratosphere and lower mesosphere using the NRL SSI, while the SORCE SSI produces a response that is larger in the lower stratosphere but out of phase with respect to total solar irradiance above 45 km.

instruction: What are the modeled responses in total ozone per 100 units of F10.7 in the tropics?
output: The modeled responses in total ozone are similar to those derived from satellite and ground-based measurements, 3- 6 Dobson Units per 100 units of 10.7-cm radio flux (F10.7) in the tropics.

instruction: What is the peak zonal mean tropical temperature response using SORCE SSI compared to NRL SSI?
output: The peak zonal mean tropical temperature response using the SORCE SSI is nearly 2 K per 100 units F10.7 - 3 times larger than the simulation using the NRL SSI.

instruction: How does the solar cycle affect the middle atmosphere temperature according to the GEOSCCM model?
output: The solar cycle in temperature is caused both through direct heating and photolysis feedbacks, processes that are mostly linearly separable.

instruction: How should chemistry-transport models simulate the solar cycle in ozone according to the findings?
output: This is important in that it means that chemistry-transport models should simulate the solar cycle in ozone well, while general circulation models without coupled chemistry will underestimate the temperature response to the solar cycle significantly in the middle atmosphere.

instruction: What dual processes affect middle atmosphere ozone and temperature according to the conclusions of the study?
output: Middle atmosphere ozone is affected almost entirely through photolysis, whereas the solar cycle in temperature is caused both through direct heating and photolysis feedbacks.

instruction: What wavelengths correspond to ozone production and destruction in the context of the solar cycle?
output: Further, the net ozone response results from the balance of ozone production at wavelengths less than 242 nm and destruction at longer wavelengths, coincidentally corresponding to the wavelength regimes of the SOLar STellar Irradiance Comparison Experiment (SOLSTICE) and Spectral Irradiance Monitor (SIM) on SORCE, respectively.

instruction: What can a higher wavelength-resolution analysis provide regarding the atmospheric response to SSI variations?
output: A higher wavelength-resolution analysis of the spectral response could allow for a better prediction of the atmospheric response to arbitrary SSI variations.

instruction: What are the five broad categories of satellite observations related to biomass burning?
output: Satellite observations related to biomass burning may be classified into five broad categories: (i) active fire location and energy release, (ii) burned areas and burn severity, (iii) smoke plume physical disposition, (iv) aerosol distribution and particle properties, and (v) trace gas concentrations.

instruction: What are the main types of quantitative measurements related to biomass burning since the launch of the Terra satellite in December 1999?

instruction: How have climate models improved in studying biomass burning activity and emissions since the introduction of quantitative satellite measurements?
output: Nevertheless, climate and other atmospheric models are making significant adjustments to take advantage of quantitative satellite measurements in studying biomass burning activity, emissions, and impacts.

instruction: What improvements are suggested for future research in the field of biomass burning and satellite observations?
output: New research directions should include not only improvements in satellite retrievals and modeling accuracies, but also increased synergy between them, such that satellite measurements can be directly input into models without requiring elaborate interpretation.

instruction: What long-term qualitative satellite datasets related to biomass burning have been available since the 1970s?
output: Some of the qualitative satellite datasets, such as fire locations, aerosol index, and gas estimates have fairly long-term records. They date back as far as the 1970s, following the launches of the DMSP, Landsat, NOAA, and Nimbus series of earth observation satellites.

instruction: What types of instruments have been launched with the new satellites from the 2000s for measuring biomass burning parameters?

instruction: What uncertainties remain in the measurements of biomass burning from satellite observations?

instruction: What do the results indicate about the biases in carbon monoxide simulations across the Arctic troposphere according to the study conducted by Monks et al. (2015)?
output: Evaluation of 11 atmospheric models with chemistry shows that they generally underestimate CO throughout the Arctic troposphere, with the largest biases found during winter and spring. Negative CO biases are also found throughout the Northern Hemisphere, with multi-model mean gross errors (9-12 %) suggesting models perform similarly over Asia, North America and Europe.

instruction: How does the multi-model annual mean tropospheric OH value reported in the study compare to previous estimates, and what implication does this have for model biases in Arctic CO?
output: A multi-model annual mean tropospheric OH (10.8 ± 0.6 × 105 molec cm−3) is found to be slightly higher than previous estimates of OH constrained by methyl chloroform, suggesting negative CO biases in models may be improved through better constraints on OH.

instruction: What discrepancies were noted in the models regarding carbon monoxide enhancements observed in the Arctic free troposphere during summer?
output: In addition to these general biases, models do not capture the magnitude of CO enhancements observed in the Arctic free troposphere in summer, suggesting model errors in the simulation of plumes that are transported from anthropogenic and biomass burning sources at lower latitudes.

instruction: What general trend is observed regarding ozone levels in the Arctic as indicated by the authors of the study?
output: O3 in the Arctic is also generally underestimated, particularly at the surface and in the upper troposphere. Summer O3 comparisons over lower latitudes show several models overestimate upper tropospheric concentrations.

instruction: What methodology did the researchers use to compare the impact of inter-model differences on carbon monoxide in the Arctic troposphere?
output: Idealised CO-like tracers are used to quantitatively compare the impact of inter-model differences in transport and OH on CO in the Arctic troposphere. The tracers show that model differences in transport.

instruction: What is the purpose of the collaboration between NASA and Dimension Technologies Inc.?

instruction: How does the new glasses-free 3D monitor assist pilots during flight?
output: The 3D capability without glasses, thanks to eye-tracking technology, should help NASA ensure pilots have all the information they need to navigate increasingly busy airports, which are already struggling with higher demand for runway space.

instruction: What advancements have been made in the glasses-free 3D monitor technology?

instruction: What are the main benefits of using a glasses-free 3D display for pilots?

instruction: What issues do pilots face with traditional two-dimensional displays in busy airspace?

instruction: What is the significance of the eye-tracking technology in DTI's monitors?

instruction: What challenges do commercial aviation pilots face regarding head positioning?

instruction: How does the DTI monitor improve the pilot's situational awareness?

instruction: In what ways have the DTI monitors been received outside of aviation?

instruction: What role does DTI envision for the 2D/3D display in future aerospace applications?

instruction: What potential markets are interested in DTI's glassless 3D technology?

instruction: How does the monitor create an immersive experience for pilots?

instruction: What role does altitude play in the properties of NOY condensation on cirrus particles?
output: Measurements of NOY condensation on cirrus particles during the SOLVE-I field campaign are analyzed and segregated based on altitude. For the data set collected on 23 January 2000, NOY condensation on cirrus particles has different properties depending on whether the ice particles are sampled in the upper troposphere, where HNO3 does not dominate NOY, or in the lower stratosphere, where HNO3 does dominate NOY.

instruction: How does HNO3 concentration vary in relation to NOY condensation on upper tropospheric ice crystals?
output: Nitric acid becomes enriched in the gas phase as NOY condenses on upper tropospheric ice crystals, indicating that a non-HNO3 component of NOY is condensing on upper tropospheric ice particles much faster and at higher concentrations than HNO3 alone on this day.

instruction: Which component of NOY is most likely condensing on upper tropospheric ice particles according to the findings?
output: It is unclear which non-HNO3 constituent of NOY is condensing on upper tropospheric ice particles, although N2O5 is the most likely species.

instruction: What conditions influence the condensation of a non-HNO3 component of NOY in the upper troposphere?
output: This condensation of a non-HNO3 component of NOY is not universal in the upper troposphere but depends on the conditions of the air parcel in which sampling occurred, notably exposure to sunlight.

instruction: What method was developed to estimate ground-level concentrations of PM2.5 mass and its constituents?
output: We develop a method that uses both the total column aerosol optical depth (AOD) and the fractional AOD values for different aerosol types, derived from Multiangle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR) aerosol data, to estimate ground-level concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) mass and its major constituents in eastern and western United States.

instruction: How does the developed method treat various MISR aerosol components?
output: Compared with previous research on linking column AOD with groundlevel PM2.5, this method treats various MISR aerosol components as individual predictor variables.

instruction: What is the sensitivity and internal consistency of MISR Version 17 aerosol microphysical properties?
output: Further analysis shows that MISR Version 17 aerosol microphysical properties have good sensitivity and internal consistency among different mixture classes.

instruction: What uncertainties are associated with distinguishing dust from non-dust particles using MISR?
output: When AOD is greater than 0.15, MISR is able to distinguish dust from non-dust particles with an uncertainty level of approximately 4%, and light-absorbing from non-light-absorbing particles with an uncertainty level of approximately 20%.

instruction: What is the retrieval uncertainty range for individual fractional AODs in the eastern and western United States?
output: The retrieval uncertainty of individual fractional AODs ranges between 5 and 11% in the eastern United States, and between 11 and 31% in the west for non-dust aerosol components.

instruction: What impact do submarine eruptions have on Earth's systems as discussed in the publication by Zheng et al. (2022)?
output: Most of Earth's volcanic eruptions occur underwater, and these submarine eruptions can significantly impact large-scale Earth systems (e.g., enhancing local primary production by phytoplankton).

instruction: What challenges exist in detecting submarine eruptions as outlined in the research by Zheng et al. (2022)?
output: However, detecting submarine eruptions is challenging due to their remote locations, short eruption durations, lack of sea surface signature (if eruptions do not breach the surface), and the transient nature of the surface manifestations of an eruption (e.g., floating pumice clasts, hydrothermal fluids).

instruction: Which satellite imagery sources are utilized for detecting new eruptions in the study conducted by Zheng et al. (2022)?
output: We can utilize global satellite imagery of 10-30 m resolution (e.g., Landsat 8, Sentinel-2) to detect new eruptions; however, the large data volumes make it challenging to systematically analyze satellite imagery globally.

instruction: What methodology was developed in the study to detect submarine eruptions?
output: In this study, we address these challenges by developing a new semi-automated analysis framework to detect submarine eruptions through supervised classification of satellite images on Google Earth Engine.

instruction: What case study was presented in the study conducted by Zheng et al. (2022)?
output: We train our algorithm using images from rafts produced by the August 2019 eruption of Volcano F in the Tofua Arc and present a case study using our methodology on satellite imagery from the Rabaul caldera region in Papua New Guinea.

instruction: What findings were made regarding pumice rafts in the study by Zheng et al. (2022)?
output: We potentially find a large number of new unreported pumice rafts (in ∼16% of images from 2017-present). After analysis of the spatial pattern of raft sightings and ancillary geophysical and visual observations, we interpret that these rafts are not the result of a new eruption.

instruction: What implications does the study suggest regarding the remobilization of pumice clasts?
output: This novel process of raft remobilization may be common at near-shore/partially submarine caldera systems (e.g., Rabaul, Krakatau) and may have significant implications for new submarine eruption detection and volcanic stratigraphy.

instruction: What were the observed changes in the advective Brewer-Dobson circulation from 1979 to 2012 according to three modern reanalyses?
output: In this work the evolution of the advective BDC for the period 1979-2012 is evaluated and compared in three modern reanalyses (ERA-Interim, MERRA, and JRA-55).

instruction: What methodology was used to compute different estimates of the Brewer-Dobson circulation in the study?
output: Three different estimates of the BDC are computed for each reanalysis, one based on the definition of the residual circulation and two indirect estimates derived from momentum and thermodynamic balances.

instruction: How much uncertainty was reported in the mean magnitude of the Brewer-Dobson circulation estimates?
output: The comparison among the nine estimates shows substantial uncertainty in the mean magnitude (∼40%) but significant common variability.

instruction: What variability factors were linked to the tropical upwelling series in the study of the Brewer-Dobson circulation?
output: The tropical upwelling series show variability linked to the stratospheric quasi-biennial oscillation and to El Niño- Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and also reflect extreme events such as major sudden stratospheric warmings and volcanic eruptions.

instruction: What was the trend analysis result concerning tropical upwelling rates from 1979-2012?
output: The trend analysis suggests a strengthening of tropical upwelling of around 2-5%/decade throughout the layer 100-10 hPa.

instruction: What did the global spatial structure of the Brewer-Dobson circulation trends indicate?
output: The global spatial structure of the BDC trends provides evidence of an overall acceleration of the circulation in both hemispheres, with qualitative agreement among the estimates.

instruction: What changes were noted regarding wave drag in both hemispheres related to Brewer-Dobson circulation trends?
output: The global BDC trends are mainly linked to changes in the boreal winter season and can be tracked to long-term increases in the resolved wave drag in both hemispheres.

instruction: Which reanalyses were compared for evaluating the advective Brewer-Dobson circulation?
output: In this work the evolution of the advective BDC for the period 1979-2012 is evaluated and compared in three modern reanalyses (ERA-Interim, MERRA, and JRA-55).

instruction: What are the implications of ozone depletion and greenhouse gas emissions on the Brewer-Dobson circulation trends?
output: Most chemistry-climate models show an intensification of the Brewer-Dobson circulation (BDC) in the stratosphere associated with increasing greenhouse gas emissions and ozone depletion in the last decades, but this trend remains to be confirmed in observational data.

instruction: What algorithm was developed to investigate the effect of the representation of aggregates on electromagnetic scattering calculations?
output: To investigate the effect of the representation of aggregates on electromagnetic scattering calculations, we developed an algorithm to efficiently specify the geometries of aggregates and to compute some of their geometric parameters, such as the projected area.

instruction: How are ice aggregates defined in this study?
output: Based on in situ observations, ice aggregates are defined as clusters of hexagonal plates with a chainlike overall shape, which may have smooth or roughened surfaces.

instruction: How many ensemble members are in the developed aggregate representation?
output: An aggregate representation is developed with 10 ensemble members, each consisting of between 4-12 hexagonal plates.

instruction: What methods are used to compute the scattering properties of an individual aggregate ice particle?
output: The scattering properties of an individual aggregate ice particle are computed using either the discrete dipole approximation or an improved geometric optics method, depending upon the size parameters.

instruction: What is the significance of the aggregate representation in satellite-based remote sensing of ice clouds?
output: Furthermore, the aggregate representation can be used to study the influence of these complex ice particles on the satellite-based remote sensing of ice clouds.

instruction: What difference does the aggregate representation make in the computed cloud reflectances?
output: The computed cloud reflectances for aggregates are different from those associated with randomly oriented individual hexagonal plates.

instruction: What result occurs when aggregates are neglected in simulations of cloud reflectances?
output: When aggregates are neglected, simulated cloud reflectances are generally lower at visible and shortwave-infrared wavelengths, resulting in smaller effective particle sizes but larger optical thicknesses.

instruction: What is the innovative method developed for oversampling satellite observations in the study?
output: An agile, physics-based oversampling approach is developed to represent each satellite observation as a sensitivity distribution on the ground, instead of a point or a polygon as assumed in previous methods.

instruction: Which satellites' observations were compared in the study to analyze oversampling errors?
output: Synthetic OMI and IASI observations were generated to compare the errors due to simplifying satellite fields of view (FOVs) as polygons (tessellation error) and the errors due to discretizing the smooth spatial response function on a finite grid (discretization error).

instruction: How does the oversampling approach affect the visualization of trace gas distribution and local gradients?
output: This physical oversampling approach is especially advantageous during smaller temporal windows and shows substantially improved visualization of trace gas distribution and local gradients when applied to OMI NO2 products and IASI NH3 products.

instruction: What is the significance of the generalized 2-D super Gaussian function in the oversampling approach?
output: The generalized 2-D super Gaussian function also enables smoothing of the level 3 results by decreasing the shape-determining exponents, which is useful for a high noise level or sparse satellite datasets.

instruction: What types of spectrometers are mentioned as being relevant for the spatial response function characterization?
output: A generalized 2-D super Gaussian function is proposed to characterize the spatial response functions of both imaging grating spectrometers (e.g., OMI, OMPS, and TROPOMI) and scanning Fourier transform spectrometers (e.g., GOSAT, IASI, and CrIS).

instruction: What advantage does the physics-based oversampling method provide compared to other methods regarding computational time?
output: There is no appreciable difference in the computational time when using the physical oversampling versus other oversampling methods.

instruction: At what grid size does oversampling using spatial response functions become beneficial for OMI?
output: For OMI, it is beneficial to oversample using the spatial response functions for grids finer than ∼ 16 km.

instruction: What is the primary goal of averaging satellite level 2 data to a level 3 grid?
output: Satellite remote sensing of the Earth's atmospheric composition usually samples irregularly in space and time, and many applications require spatially and temporally averaging the satellite observations (level 2) to a regular grid (level 3).

instruction: What are the two sources of error analyzed in the oversampling method?
output: The balance between these two error sources depends on the target grid size, the ground size of the FOV, and the smoothness of spatial response functions.

instruction: What innovations in liquid cooling technology were originally developed for NASA spacesuits?
output: In the mid-1960s, NASA adopted for the Apollo lunar suits a concept originally developed by the British Royal Air Force to provide cooling for aircraft pilots in hot environments. It utilized a battery-operated miniature pump that cycled chilled water through a series of tubes lining the garment, which pressed against the skin, absorbing heat. An iteration of this liquid cooling technology is still used by astronauts today.

instruction: How do Vasper Systems' liquid-cooled compression cuffs improve exercise efficiency?
output: Utilizing that theory, Wasowski developed his own compression cuffs that also incorporate the NASA-derived liquid cooling technology, which, in addition to increasing one's exercise efficiency, also helps to reduce sweat and post-workout aches and tiredness.

instruction: What are the key benefits of anaerobic exercise highlighted in the article?
output: The benefits of anaerobic exercise are many, as it builds muscles and strength, burns fat, increases anabolic hormones (human growth hormone, testosterone), continues the burning of calories after exercise through excess post-oxygen consumption, and enhances endurance by increasing lactate threshold and maximal oxygen consumption, or VO2 max. According to Wasowski, these benefits are superior to those offered by aerobic exercise.

instruction: What is the purpose of the 'RICE' method in athletic injury treatment?
output: When someone sprains his or her knee or ankle, the RICE (rest, ice, compression, and elevation) method is standard protocol for treating such an injury. Icing plays a critical role in reducing pain and swelling, but applying ice for too long or with too cold a compress can cause more tissue damage.

instruction: How does Vasper Systems' exercise program accommodate individuals unable to perform traditional anaerobic activities?
output: The low-impact nature of the Vasper exercise protocol also leads to decreased wear and tear on the body compared to more physically strenuous routines. That also means the typical delayed muscled soreness that frequently comes after exercise is avoided. This makes the Vasper program highly accessible to those recovering from injury or vulnerable due to age or disease.

instruction: What physiological effects did NASA Ames Research Center explore regarding cooling technologies?
output: Starting in the late 1960s, a team of scientists and engineers at NASA Ames Research Center investigated the physiological effects of a wide variety of artificial cooling concepts. Many of these were subsequently commercially developed and applied to solve various industrial, military, and medical problems on Earth.

instruction: What is the significance of cooling technology for astronaut safety?
output: The human body in space is as vulnerable as a fish out of water. Beyond a spacecraft's protective environment, there is no oxygen to breathe and nothing to shield you from the sun's searing heat and radiation. And just as disturbing, the lack of air pressure means your body suffers from rapid decompression symptoms and eventual death.

instruction: Which markets are utilizing the NASA-derived liquid cooling technology today?
output: Professional athletes, therapy centers, and athletic trainers around the world now use the technology.

instruction: How does the Vasper workout protocol compare in duration to traditional workouts?
output: A Vasper session takes only 30 minutes to compete, which reflects, Wasowski says, the efficiency of the technologies built into it.

instruction: What future health outcomes are being explored with cool compression technology?
output: The cool compression technology's effects on other health outcomes are also being explored, for instance, on those who suffer from Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis, and for patients undergoing cardiac rehabilitation.

instruction: What is the significance of convection for redistributing trace gases in the troposphere according to the ARCTAS aircraft campaign?
output: Observations of a comprehensive suite of inorganic and organic trace gases, including non-methane hydrocarbons (NMHCs), halogenated organics, and oxygenated volatile organic compounds (OVOCs), obtained from the NASA DC-8 over Canada during the ARCTAS aircraft campaign in July 2008 illustrate that convection is important for redistributing both long- and short-lived species throughout the troposphere.

instruction: What were the observed mixing ratios of organic species in the upper troposphere during convective outflow events?
output: Convective outflow events were identified by the elevated mixing ratios of organic species in the upper troposphere relative to background conditions.

instruction: How does isoprene affect OH levels when convected without lightning NOx?
output: When convective storms transport isoprene from the boundary layer to the upper troposphere and no LNOx is present, OH is reduced due to scavenging by isoprene, which serves to slow the chemistry, resulting in longer lifetimes for species that react with OH. Ozone and PAN production is minimal in this case.

instruction: What are the consequences of convecting isoprene in the presence of lightning NOx for upper tropospheric chemistry?
output: In the case where isoprene is convected and LNOx is present, there is a large effect on the expected ensuing chemistry: isoprene exerts a dominant impact on HOx and nitrogen-containing species; the relative contribution from other species to HOx, such as peroxides, is insignificant.

instruction: What primary and secondary products result from the reaction of isoprene in the upper troposphere?
output: The isoprene reacts quickly, resulting in primary and secondary products, including formaldehyde and methyl glyoxal.

instruction: What products and outcomes does the model predict when LNOx is present along with isoprene?
output: The model predicts enhanced production of alkyl nitrates (ANs) and peroxyacyl nitrate compounds (PANs). PANs persist because of the cold temperatures of the upper troposphere resulting in a large change in the NOx mixing ratios which, in turn, has a large impact on the HOx chemistry.

instruction: What was the net gain of ozone production measured after the convection of isoprene in comparison to scenarios without isoprene?
output: Ozone production is substantial during the first few hours following the convection to the UT, resulting in a net gain of approximately 10 ppbv compared to the modeled scenario in which LNOx is present but no isoprene is present aloft.

instruction: What event was caused by forest fires in British Columbia in August 2017?
output: Forest fires in British Columbia in August 2017 caused a pyrocumulonimbus event that injected a polluted air mass into the lower stratosphere.

instruction: When did the Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) first observe the polluted air mass from Canadian forest fires?
output: The Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) on the Aura satellite first observed the polluted air mass on 14 August 2017 and continued to observe it for 60 d (100 d in water vapour).

instruction: What is the estimated mass of carbon monoxide (CO) injected into the stratosphere during the August 2017 Canadian forest fires?
output: We estimate the mass of CO injected into the stratosphere to be 2400 Gg.

instruction: How many events of direct injection of burning products into the stratosphere have occurred since the launch of Aura?
output: Events in which a fire injects its burning products directly into the stratosphere are rare: this is the third of four such events in the 16 years since the launch of Aura, the second largest of the four events, and the only one in the Northern Hemisphere.

instruction: What was the water vapor content of the polluted air mass observed in August 2017 compared to the surrounding atmosphere?
output: Unlike the 2006 and 2009 events, but like the 2019-2020 event, the polluted air mass described here had a clearly elevated water vapour content: between 2.5 and 5 times greater than that in the surrounding atmosphere.

instruction: At what altitude did the polluted air mass rise during the August 2017 event?
output: We describe the evolution of the polluted air mass, showing that it rose to an altitude of about 24 km (31 hPa) and divided into several identifiable parts.

instruction: What pollutants besides CO and H2O were observed by MLS in the polluted air mass?
output: In addition to CO and H2 O, we observe enhanced amounts of HCN, CH3 CN, CH3 Cl and CH3 OH with mixing ratios in the range to be expected from a variety of measurements in other biomass burning plumes.

instruction: Where did the pollutants observed by MLS originate during the Canadian forest fires?
output: We use back trajectories and plume-dispersion modelling to demonstrate that the pollutants observed by MLS originated in the British Columbia fires, the likeliest source being at 53.2◦ N, 121.8◦ W at 05:20 UTC on 13 August 2017.

instruction: What instrument is used to observe biomass burning products in the stratosphere?
output: The Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) on the Aura satellite first observed the polluted air mass on 14 August 2017.

instruction: What scientific publication reported the MLS observations of biomass burning products in August 2017?
output: Pumphrey, H. , M. Schwartz , M. Santee , P. Kablick , M. Fromm , and N. Livesey (2021), Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) observations of biomass burning products in the stratosphere from Canadian forest fires in August 2017, Atmos. Chem. Phys. , 21 , 16645-16659, doi:10.5194/acp-21-16645-2021.

instruction: What conclusion is drawn about the optical effect of microscopic dust on wavelength-sized particles?

instruction: What opportunity does the Sub-Mesoscale Ocean Dynamics Experiment (S-MODE) provide in relation to ocean forecast systems?
output: The recent Sub-Mesoscale Ocean Dynamics Experiment (S-MODE) provides an opportunity to examine the data assimilation issues that can limit predictive skill.

instruction: What was the unique system used to provide high resolution observations during the ocean forecast experiments?
output: A unique swarm control system guided nine ocean gliders accounting for all satellite and in situ data to provide high resolution observations for three ocean forecast experiments.

instruction: How did the assimilation adaptation improve temperature skill in ocean forecasts?
output: When measured by spatial scales along the glider paths, skill in temperature advances from scales larger than about 220 km wavelength when utilizing the glider data with prior assimilation down to scales larger than 80 km wavelength with the adaptive assimilation.

instruction: What were the advancements in skill for salinity using the adaptive assimilation method?
output: Skill in salinity advances from scales of approximately 300 km to scales of 200 km.

instruction: What results were implied regarding ocean observing systems and ocean forecast systems?
output: The results imply that as ocean observing systems advance, ocean forecast systems must adapt to use local high resolution observations.

instruction: What data was used to confirm the findings in the ocean forecast experiments?
output: Additionally, conductivity, temperature, and depth observations from an EcoCTD instrument provide independent data for confirmation.

instruction: What types of data were assimilated in the first ocean forecast experiment?
output: The first ocean forecast experiment had no glider data assimilated.

instruction: What are the benefits of using an adaptive assimilation technique compared to prior methods?
output: The assimilation adaptation used a spatially varying horizontal decorrelation scale enabling corrections at smaller scales where high resolution in situ data are concentrated.

instruction: By how much did the skill in steric height improve with adaptive assimilation?
output: Skill in steric height advances from 140 km to 63 km.

instruction: What specific mission is associated with the research conducted in this publication?
output: Mission: S-MODE.

instruction: What were the main research objectives of the ARCTAS and ARCPAC field campaigns conducted in 2008?
output: In the spring of 2008 NASA and NOAA funded the ARCTAS and ARCPAC field campaigns as contributions to POLARCAT, a core IPY activity.

instruction: How many hours of in-situ sampling were conducted by the aircraft during the ARCTAS/ARCPAC campaigns?
output: During the campaigns the NASA DC-8, P-3B and NOAA WP-3D aircraft conducted over 160 h of in-situ sampling between 0.1 and 12 km throughout the Western Arctic north of 55◦ N (i.e. Alaska to Greenland).

instruction: What types of measurements were taken by the aircraft during the ARCTAS/ARCPAC campaigns?
output: All aircraft were equipped with multiple wavelength measurements of aerosol optics, trace gas and aerosol chemistry measurements, as well as direct measurements of the aerosol size distributions and black carbon mass.

instruction: What contribution did Asian biomass burning emissions make to the black carbon burden in the Western Arctic?
output: Though these smoke plumes account for only 11-14 % of the samples within the Western Arctic domain, they account for 42-47 % of the total burden of black carbon.

instruction: What is the estimated mass absorption efficiency for black carbon at 470 nm, 530 nm, and 660 nm wavelengths?
output: Stratifying the data to reduce the influence of dust allows us to determine mass absorption efficiencies for black carbon of 11.2±0.8, 9.5±0.6 and 7.4±0.7 m2 g−1 at 470, 530 and 660 nm wavelengths.

instruction: What is the estimated mass absorption efficiency for brown carbon at 470 nm and 530 nm wavelengths?
output: We derive mass absorption efficiencies for brown carbon of 0.83±0.15 and 0.27±0.08 m2 g−1 at 470 and 530 nm wavelengths.

instruction: What was the contribution of dust to total light absorption at 470 nm and 530 nm wavelengths above 6 km?
output: Dust was also commonly observed but only contributes to 4-12 % and 3-8 % of total light absorption at 470 and 530 nm wavelengths above 6 km.

instruction: What challenges were faced in estimating the absorption efficiency for dust?
output: However the absorption efficiency estimates for dust are highly uncertain due to the limitations imposed by PSAP instrument noise.

instruction: What critical knowledge gaps do the ARCTAS/ARCPAC measurements address regarding absorbing aerosol over the Western Arctic?
output: In-situ ARCTAS/ARCPAC measurements during the IPY provide valuable constraints for absorbing aerosol over the Western Arctic, species which are currently poorly simulated over a region that is critically under-sampled.
